speechtext: House in committee to consider Bill (No. 153) to incorporate the Saskatchewan Power Company.-Mr. McCraney.

I do not desire to take any strong objection to this Bill, if it is the view of the committee that it should pass. But I would call attention to the fact that it is purely local in its character. It is a Bill to incorporate a company for the development of a water power on the Saskatchewan river, simply in one province. I would think myself that this is peculiarly an undertaking which ought to be under the control of the province, and that the company ought to be incorporated by the province. I do not know whether the committee to which the Bill was referred has given that matter consideration. My own view would be that progress should be reported, and that this point should be considered. If we keep on, we may before long be in conflict with the province of Saskatchewan, just as we are with the province of Ontario.
This Bill proposes to deal with a navigable stream. I do not think it would be under the jurisdiction of tile province.

I raised the same question on Friday last when this Bill was before the committee. X quite agree with what the Minister of Public Works has said.
I think this is purely a provincial matter, but I may be mistaken. One of the members for Saskatchewan gave an explanation the other day, and perhaps he will repeat it to-day. To my mind, this is a provincial matter, and should not be dealt with here.

If I may be allowed to give an illustration of the mode in which questions like this should be dealt with-in the province of New Brunswick we have frequently incorporated companies to construct works of this, character, to establish booms and that sort of thing in navigable rivers, and then the company avails itself of the provision of the federal law which requires that before interfering with a navigable river there shall be an approval of the works by the Minister of Public Works for Canada. But the incorporation of the company, it seems to me, properly belongs to the provincial legislature, because by the terms of the British North America Act a provincial legislature is exclusively invested with power to incorporate companies for carrying on local undertakings with local objects.

I understand the objection of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugslev) is based on the ground that the incorporation of the gentlemen who are named here should be undertaken by the province, and that then permission should be obtained from the Dominion parliament for the use of those waters.
From the Minister of Public Works, under the revised statutes relating to navigable waters.

By this Bill we are coming here for the authority of the Dominion parliament to use the waters of the South Saskatchewan river under terms which are set forth in the Bill. True, we could go to the provincial legislature and get incorporation, 'but that would involve a delay, which we desire to avoid. This Parliament could give the rights which we ask to individuals, who could assign those rights which they acquire to a company to be incorporated by the provincial legislature. I think, however, it is much better that we in this parliament who give the right to make use of the river, should also incorporate the persons to whom it is intended that these powers should be given as a corporate body, and that we should set forth the powers which are incidental to that incorporation. If the minister wishes to Mr. PUGSLEY.
have it stand for further consideration, I can offer no objection.

I observe that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) who looks after these Bills is not here at the moment. As I understand, this insurance company operated under a provincial charter. There are contractual engagements, of course, which will be limited by the provincial law. But the effect of this Bill will be to leave them free of these and place them under federal jurisdiction.

This Bill provides that all the liabilities of the old company shall remain as liabilities, notwithstanding that it comes under this proposed Dominion law. One clause of the Bill particularly discussed in the Banking and Commerce Committee was that providing that calls might be made on the stock to the extent of 25 per cent. The original Manitoba charter was consulted, and it was found that it provided that calls should be limited to 10 per cent. It was thought unfair to saddle the shareholders with larger calls than had been provided for under the original Act. And so the clause permitting the 25 per cent call was changed to 10 per cent in the present Bill-

Everything in the measure was carefully considered.

I do not know what the insurance law of Manitoba provides, but I know that under the Ontario law an insurance company such as this is allowed to make only a certain contract with the Insured party-it cannot" contract itself out of certain liabilities. X do not know whether there is such a law in force in Manitoba. But the effect of this Bill would be to remove that safeguard, if it exists, from those who have insured with this company, by transferring the company to federal jurisdiction.

Their longest contract of insurance would be for three years, and a large number of them would be for twelve months or less. So, this would not be so serious a matter as in the case of a life insurance company. [DOT]

To the Editor of the ' Chronicle/
Sir,-Kindly allow me space in your valuable paper to express my views re the coasting trade and the Norwegian question or foreign shipping monopolizing our coasting trade. It is a difficult question to solve or bring to a satisfactory settlement and I believe if not settled it will lead to anarchy and rebellion in the end, as it is a terrible grievance for our vessels to lay at coal piers and steamers load and go away and return and load again and our vessels laying^ without cargoes or any recompense for their lost time as I have had the experience of it a number of times. Now I am aware that the companies have to have steamers to carry their coal. Also, do I know they have a right to charter wherever they can make the best bargain. I am opposed to unions and monopolies as they tend to coerce the freedom and rights of individual citizens, and my idea of bringing this vexed question to a satisfactory settlement is for the government to compel all coal companies to load all vessels in turn, no preference to steam over sailing tonnage, as all have equal rights. I have loaded coal a number of times for the last twenty years in American ports and never had to wait long for my cargo as everything was loaded in turn, steamer, barge or sailing vessel and no reasonable man^ will complain when he gets his turn or lights. This is my view for a satisfactory settlement ot the trouble or grievance.
ALEX. WEATHERBEE. Tatamagouehe, Dec. 21, 1S07.

I understand that it is a moot question whether the federal authorities have power to deal with this matter or whether the power rests with the legislature of the province of Nova Scotia. But I think this matter is one which peculiarly lies within the powers of the parliament of Canada to deal with. This is not a matter of purely local importance, because vessels from various provinces of Canada habitually load at these piers. It is true, these companies, or most of them, are chartered by the legislature of the province of Nova Scotia; but notwithstanding that fact, I think this parliament has power to regulate the manner in which vessels shall be loaded and unloaded at these piers. Under the shipping laws of the Dominion of Canada all the regulations for the unloading of vessels are subject to the parliament of Canada. If this parliament has power to regulate the unloading of vessels, I do not see why it should not equally have power to regulate the loading of vessels. It has power under the federal shipping law to say what space shall be allotted for cattle on vessels, how many bushels of grain a vessel may carry, how much draft it may draw, etc. Why, then, should it not have power to regulate the manner in which vessels from Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec shall be loaded at these piers? It may be and probably will be said that these concerns are private concerns, and can make contracts to load as they please. Vessels from all parts of Canada come to these places for coal. Under the circumstances, this is a matter of federal importance which may come under the head of regulation of trade and commerce, subsection 2 of section 91 British North America Act. Why should not this parliament have the power, under that section, to regulate the manner in which vessels shall be loaded, the same as they regulate, under subsection 10, which deals with navigation and shipping, the manner in which vessels shall lie in the harbour or conduct themselves at a pier. Under these regulations, no vessel is permitted to carry any spars clear of her hull because that might interfere with other vessels coming in.

Under what clause of the British North America Act?

Under clause 2 of section 91 dealing with the regulation of trade and commerce. Take, for instance, section 92 which defines what matters come within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature. Under that section, shop, saloon, tavern and auctioneer and other licenses, in order to the raising of revenue for provincial, local or municipal purposes come under the exclusive powers of the provincial legislature. This trouble of the detention of vessels at piers at the various mines is an old grievance in the coal trade. I remember some years ago when there were a good many sailing vessels in the business, that frequently at the larger coal piers and shipping points there was a detention to some sailing vessels sometimes of five or six weeks, occasioned by other sailing vessels and larger ships getting a preference in obtaining cargoes of coal for larger ports of consumption. At a certain time of the year large sailing ships took cargoes for the St. Lawrence, and as the period of navigation closed at a certain time, it was necessary to give them despatcli in order that they might reach their destination on the St. Lawrence in time. Undoubtedly a grievance existed. In my opinion a remedy might be found in two ways.
What does the bon. gentleman make of this statement I have read?

I will come to that in a moment. I am now speaking of the conditions which existed twenty or thirty years or more ago. There was also more or less detention at coal piers owing to the circumstances I have mentioned. The great grievance which existed then was that when steamers began to ply in the coal trade and came to a pier, the master of the pier, or dock master, prevented the sailing vessels which had taken part of a cargo from taking the rest of it. Frequently when a vessel was partially loaded, steamers came in and the vessel had to haul away from under the coal chute without obtaining her cargo. Now if a certain number of chutes at these larger piers were devoted to serving small vessels, a great part of the grievance would be removed.
Another regulation might be made that no steamer ought to return and take on a second cargo until the vessels which were present at the pier before she loaded are loaded. As has been observed by my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. A. A. McLean), it is a great vexation and annoyance to the masters of vessels lying at piers for them

to observe one of these steamers being filled with a cargo, perhaps ten times as much as these vessels hold, take her cargo up the St. Lawrence and come back again before these vessels have been loaded. The advent of the big cargo steamers has made a great change in the coal trade. The requirements of the St. Lawrence, no doubt, demanded vessels of a larger size. Formerly the largest cargo was probably 1,000 tons, but to-day, there are these Norwegian steamers that carry 6,000 tons. Some of the mines have so arranged that they shall have a steamer under the chutes all the time and that means that vessels that intervene can get no loads, because, when one steamer is loaded and moves away, another one takes her place ; this goes on in rotation and the result is that these smaller vessels are not. loaded. It is true that these vessels carrying large cargoes are under foreign flags, largely the Norwegian flag, but how this government is to intervene and prevent the owners of the mines from transporting their own products in their own way, I do not know. I do not know that the remedy is in the hands of the government. But, there is a question in regard to the supply of the St. Lawrence -the supply of Montreal and Quebec- and that is that these large centres require large quantities of coal and as a result a difficulty arises in connection with supplying the smaller ports in Nova Scotia. Before the period of navigation closes these large centres must obtain their coal and. notwithstanding that they have a large supply of tonnage, there are ports in the maritime provinces that receive no coal. Not only is there a grievance on the part of the owners of the small vessels but there is a grievance on the part of the smaller ports because the consumers of coal in these places do not receive the product that they require. They are practically the owners of the coal themselves as being resident in the province of Nova Scotia which is blessed by having a large supply and they naturally feel that they have a grievance because, as owners of the product under the ground, they are not in a position to receive the supply which they require and because they have to pay a larger price for that commodity. I do not intend to enter into the legal question or to discuss the point as to whether this government can provide a remedy for this grievance. The grievance undoubtedly does exist. It may partly remedy it to provide that no steamer shall receive her second cargo until the vessels that are at the piers at the time of her loading receive the quantity they require. Whether this government can enforce a regulation of that kind or whether it is the prerogative of the local government, I do not know. But, there is a very strong objection urged : Why should not the proprietor of the coal mine be able to sell and provide for the convey-Mr. W. ROCHE.

In olden times, when there was too great an accumulation of vessels at the mines, the mine owners themselves stopped the delivery to vessels going foreign. Newfoundland sealers and vessels that made sea voyages came over to North Sydney and no other vessels could obtain cargo. connection no person would be better pleased than myself, but, like all other lines of business I think that this mining business will adjust itself. There was hitherto considerable competition among the Nova Scotia coal companies for the St. Lawrence market but fortunately for the coal trade and for the owners of sailing vessels the growth and extent of the local market which is supplied by the sailing vessels, is convincing the coal producers that it is fast becoming a very valuable market and that it requires recognition from them. This question has been frequently discussed in the press of the maritime provinces and in the legislatures as well. The hon. gentleman who brought the matter to the attention of the House has not seen fit to suggest to the minister-that is providing this parliament has any power to deal with the question-any remedy. It has been said that in the United States certain customs exist at the coal loading ports, but as to that we have no evidence, and it does seem as if, before the subject was brought forward as it has been, the hon. gentlemen from Prince Edward Island should have been able to suggest some remedy for the grievance. For various reasons, last year was a peculiar year in the coal trade of Nova Scotia. Owing to the lateness of the opening of navigation on the St. Lawrence the coal companies could not begin to fill their
contracts until late in June, and as the trade with the St. Lawrence has been increasing greatly during the past ten years, and as there were very large orders last year, the time for the delivery of the coal was more limited than in previous years. Again, in the Springhill mines in Cumberland county, one of the largest coal producing mines in Nova Scotia outside of the island of Cape Breton, there was a strike, and in consequence there was a tremendous demand on the capacity of the mines in Pictou county, Inverness county, and Cape Breton county. While these gentlemen who have written in the press so vigorously had doubtless a grievance, yet it is only fair to remember the conditions under which the coal trade of the province was conducted last year. In conjunction with the causes I have mentioned, there is the further cause that the small consumers in the various provinces locally, did not attempt to get their supply of coal until late in the season, and having waited with their orders until the last minute there was more difficulty in supplying them. I do not think any one has the- right to assume that the coal companies deliberately intend to discriminate in this matter. Under ordinary conditions and if the opportunities for shipping were normal in each year, there is no doubt that the coal companies would do all in their power to supply anybody and everybody who might come along. We have had a great development in the coal trade of Nova Scotia in recent years, a developuent which did not take place during the time our friends opposite were in power although they claimed to be the friends of the coal industry ; a development which awaited the coining into power of the present government. Then coal areas which for many years remained untouched were brought into operation, and as a consequence new companies were pressing for business and making contracts to sell coal here and there so as to dispose of the immensely increased production. I might point out that the complaints which my hon. friends have given vent to to-day have no bearing against the coal companies in the county I have the honour to represent, or in the county of Cape Breton, but were confined to the county of Inverness. In proof of the fact that tiiere was some discrimination there a letter was produced from the manager of one of the mines to the effect that it was impossible for them to supply coal locally until the St. Lawrence was frozen over, which meant that this Inverness Coal and Railway Company had taken large contracts in Montreal which under the conditions of the shortened season of navigation it was encumbent on them to fill. Taking into account the abnormal season of last year and the deferring until the last minute of local coal orders, the natural result was that vessel owners might expect some difficulty in getting supplies. But they were not the only

As a matter of fact, I can tell my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island that I will undertake to be answerable for any coal companies in Pictou county, that they will supply all the schooners that can be sent over this summer.

Were there no representations made to my hon. friend ?
If you know what the representations were, tell it.
I have an idea.
An idea ? You have no idea in your head.
It is getting a little too warm for my hon. friend ; but he must not complain if he is told the truth, occasionally

So far as I am concerned, I want to tell the hon. gentleman that no representations were made to me except those which come from the legislature of Prince Edward Island and from the captains whose petition I read to the House.
I can say the same thing, and I would like to know now what representations the hon. gentleman refers to.

I understood that my hon. friends from Prince Edward Island were speaking this afternoon as a result of certain representations which had been made to them. If no representations have been made to them, I can quite understand their position. I take it, then, that the fact that no representations have been made to them accounts for the extraordinary position they take.
I do not want the hon. gentleman to put words into my mouth. I told him distinctly that no representations were made to me except what I referred to when I spoke.
Then I am to assume that representations were made to my hon. friend in regard to this matter. If representations had been made to my hon. friend, as I am bound to assume they were
Your representations don't fit.

I was right, it is evident, when I assumed earlier that the facts were the last thing my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Martin) desired with regard to this question. It was not a remedy for this alleged grievance that my hon. friend desired.
What representations does the hon. gentleman refer to ? I do not know what he means.

I am satisfied now none were made to my hon. friend. Alter he had finished his operations a little while ago, I came to the conclusion that none had been made to him. His remarks showed such an absolute want of knowledge on the question, that I cannot imagine he had received any representations. As my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has pointed out, the immediate question arose in connection with the difficulty at Port Hastings last fall. As my hon. friend has pointed out, the Dominion Coal Company have made special provisions for attending to the class of shipping referred to this afternoon. Some years ago a question arose of alleged discrimination against sailing vessels, but steps were taken by those interested to provide a remedy. Representations, for instance, had been made to myself, but when they were, I did not take the course followed by my hon. friend. I did not conceal the representations in my pocket, but went with them to the people who could remedy the grievance. I went to the operators of the mines in Nova Scotia and Cape Bretou, who are reasonable people ; and I may tell my hon. friend something perhaps he does not know, and that is that every coal operator in Nova Scotia is anxious to accommodate this particular trade of which he speaks. It is a profitable trade for them. There is not a coal operator who would not be pleased to be in a position to deal with it. I made representations some three or four years ago to the Dominion) Coal Company, and that company took steps to provide specially for the accommodation of this particular class of traffic about which my hon. friend is so much concerned. I can tell him that the Dominion Coal Company all last year were advertising in the newspapers for schooners to come to the coal pier which the company had constructed specially for the accommodation of this class of shipping, and a large number of these schooners did come. The company were prepared to accommodate more than they were able to get. At the other piers of the company there were from time to time people who represented that they had not been properly treated. I made representations to the company, and they assured me that during the coming season they will, at least three days in the week, give preference to the particular class of craft referred to. If my hon. friend had been interested in this question in any other respect than as a grievance, he -would have sought some information from the people engaged in the trade, and he would have found out that they are making provision to the best of their ability for the accommodation of this traffic. My hon. friend ought to know that the coal companies in Nova Scotia have, in order to keep their men about them, to go into the markets in advance and sell their coal. They

go out months in advance in order to find a market and enter into contracts for the supply of coal, and if they fail to deliver according to contract they are under a forfeit. And it might well happen that when a schooner arrives on a certain day, there is no coal available on that particular day because the company has already sold that day's supply and is under contract to deliver it to a buyer who bought it perhaps months in advance. These are some of the difficulties. They were correctly outlined by my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Roche) a short time ago, when he pointed out that it is somewhat difficult to say to any company engaged in coal mining that it cannot make provision for the sale and transportation of its own coal. The coal companies charter their own fleets of steamers, sell their own coal, and carry it on those steamers. In no other way can they successfully conduct their operations. The St. Lawrence market is the one upon which, in the main, the collieries of Nova Scotia depend, and the main portion of the coal mined in Nova Scotia must be marketed in the St. Lawrence, and marketed not by the particular class of craft referred to, but by large steamers. So far as the grievances of the schooners are concerned, they have been removed as far as possible. I have consulted not alone the Dominion Coal Company but other proprietors in Nova Scotia, and they all assure me that they were willing to go to the extent to accommodate this particular class of vessels.' During the coming season they are going to lay themselves out still further to meet the demands made upon them. I would say to my hon. friend, the Postmaster General, who wrote me a short time ago, that I have directed the attention of the Dominion Coal Company in my county to the representations made by him. The general sales agent of the company assured me not later than last night, that if schooners from the constituency of the Postmaster General were in need of coal, he would be prepared to accommodate them during the coming season. Any impartial observer who takes the trouble to ascertain the facts, must admit that reasonable efforts are being made by the coal companies to meet the demands upon them.

I do not wish to interfere in the debate except to say that a few days ago I received a letter from the local member for the Magdalen Islands complaining of the trouble experienced in the last few years in getting coal from the collieries in Cape Breton, and he wanted me to see my hon. friend who represents Cape Breton (Mr. Johnston) and endeavour to have satisfactory provisions made for the future. After talking the matter over with my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. Johnston) and my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), I was glad to learn that they will Mr. JOHNSTON.
do their best with the collieries so as to have the people from Magdalen Island accommodated. I have the fullest confidence in my hon. friend's judgment and good intentions, and the electors of Magdalen Island will be glad to know that in the future they will get their coal at the earliest opportunity.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. J. HUGHES (Kings, P. E. I.).
speechtext:
There is no doubt that the owners and masters of small sailing vessels who were detained for weeks last autumn at Port Hastings and some other places where they were accustomed to get coal, and finally had to leave without cargoes, while they saw steamers arriving long after they had arrived, get cargoes and leave-there is no doubt that these men were subjected to loss and hardship and annoyance. They lost a trip of their vessels ; they had to disappoint the customers to whom they expected to supply coal ; and they had the annoyance of waiting there for some weeks and leaving, in many cases, without coal. This is a somewhat difficult thing to remedy. It appears that the demand for coal last year, at some of the coal ports was unusually large. This is one of the signs of the ' growing time.' I suppose that, in a growing country like this, where the demand for coal is increasing rapidly every year, some inconvenience will be experienced, particularly when vessels leave it somewhat late in the year before applying for their usual coal supply. The masters of these vessels did a reasonable thing, a natural thing, in applying where they thought they might find a remedy, in making their grievances known, in applying to the legislatures, and to the members of parliament. And the knowledge obtained in that way has perhaps resulted, or will result, in bringing about a remedy. For my own part, I have received several representations from captains on this subject. I have also received a resolution passed by the legislature of Prince Edward Island, and a resolution passed by the Board of Trade of Charlottetown. I have brought these resolutions to the notice of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and to the notice of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), because he is one of the ministers from the maritime provinces. But it appears to me that there was great difficulty in the government interfering in private business of that kind, and saying when and how and to whom the coal mine owners should sell coal, and in what way they should sell it. I am not learned in the law, but still I could see a difficulty in any government interfering in private business. Of course, I can imagine a condition of things arising that would be so important to the country that the government would be obliged to interfere for the greatest good of the people. But that condition, I am satisfied, has not yet arisen.

Now, in order to arrive at something practical in the way of a settlement of this difficulty during the present year, I made it my business to meet some of the directers of the coal companies from which the people of Prince Edward Island get their supplies. Mr. McLean, a director of the Port Hood mines was one of the directors I met. I represented this matter to him, and found that he had been considering it himself and with his co-directors. He told me that he was very much impressed with the representations that I and others made on the subject. He said that he believed his company in the future, would pay more attention to the supply of domestic consumers. They were looking at it from a business standpoint, and realizing that the domestic consumption of coal was increasing every year and would continue to increase, and that it would be a permanent demand, whereas by industrial concerns consumption of coal at Montreal or some of the other great points might be large one year and might fall off another year for causes, perhaps, general in their operations, he considered that it would be better for his company, which was supplying a good quality of coal, to cater first to the local domestic consumption, and then give the surplus, whatever it might be, to the industrial corporations in the large centres. He told me that, so far as his company was concerned, he believed it would pursue that course next year, and probably in the years to come. I also had occasion to speak to Mr. Mann, of the firm of Mackenzie & Mann, the owners of the Inverness mines. The Inverness coal, I may say, has an excellent reputation as a coal for domestic consumption; the people like to get it wherever it is possible to do so. And this was the colliery that caused the greatest congestion of sailing vessels last year. I pointed out the case to Mr. Mann. He told me that the company had had large orders for coal from the great consuming centres, such as Montreal and others; but he, too, recognized the importance of the domestic demand, and informed me that his company were taking steps to meet this domestic demand during the coming season. He thought that all reasonable objections would he removed, and intimated that, as far as possible, the local men should apply for their coal as early as possible in the season. Now, I think this was a practical way of going to work and a practical way of finding a remedy. I do not, of course, object to lion, gentlemen bringing up the matter in their own way and taking up a good deal of the time of parliament, but I really think the good work was all done before this afternoon and before the matter was brought up in the House. I am convinced that the grievance-a real grievance -that we complained of last year will be largely removed this year by the action of the coalmine owners themselves. And, if
that can be brought about, that is a practical way and the best way of doing it. If that cannot be brought about, and if there is great hardship inflicted upon the people for the want of coal, I presume that parliament would have to interfere. But I hope and trust-and I believe-that such a condition will not arise.

I have heard complaints in my constituency similar to that made by the two hon. members for Prince Edward Island this afternoon. But, whatever be the justification for these complaints, I submit that it is not a fair matter for discussion in this House [DOT] and I suspect very strongly that the hon. gentlemen opposite who have spoken regarding the alleged discrimination, against sailing vessels are rather interested in votes than in coal. I cannot imagine what authority this parliament would have to deal with the subject. It is clearly a case which would come within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature. I assume that this might very easily be done by an amendment of the charter of the various coal companies operating in Nova Scotia.
Now, this matter was discussed in the Nova Scotia provincial assembly just a few weeks ago. One of the chief promoters of the agitation against certain of the collieries of Nova Scotia was Mr. Moses H. Nickerson, who moved a resolution asking the Nova Scotia legislature to inquire into this grievance and as to the facts alleged against the collieries. In moving his resolution, he expressly stated that, upon investigation, the charges related only to the Inverness Coal and Railway Company. That resolution was supported by the legislature of Nova Scotia unanimously. It was accepted bv the premier of Nova Scotia. The resolution asked that the government take steps to ascertain the facts, and then, after learning all the facts, to deal with it if the facts seemed to justify intervention. The Premier of Nova Scotia, in closing his remarks, states :
However the situation might he in that particular, he was personally only too pleased to endorse the resolution calling upon the government to take steps to ascertain the facts, and after they obtained the facts they could determine the remedy, if any there was, under the powers of the provincial government.
Now, I submit that it is the provincial government of Nova Scotia alone which can deal with an issue of this kind, and that seems to be the opinion of the members of the legislature of that province, on both sides. In looking at the discussion upon this question I was impressed with a statement made by the member for Inverness, who I think put the matter very well, and 1 along the same lines as was done this after-

noon by tlie member for Inverness (Mr. McLennan) :
Hon. Mr. Macdonald said he was in full sympathy with the owners of schooners employed in carrying; coal, and when this agitation was coming on he thought the coal companies were at fault, and in order to satisfy himself he made a private investigation into the matter. One thing he found wa= that owing to the lateness of the spring last year the coal companies-he referred particularly to the Inverness and Richmond Company-notified their customers in the maritime provinces that they were prepared to load anv class of vessels with' despatch in the month of .May and up to the time that navigation opened in the St. Lawrence, but they met with no response. As a matter of fact, up to the middle of June, very little shipping was done. It must be remembered that in order to keep their mines in operation they had to make contracts for the delivery of coal np the St. Lawrence, as had all the companies in the island of Cape Breton, and they sent that notification out for the purpose of relieving the pressure when navigation opened in the St. Lawrence so that they would be that much ahead. But there was no response to the notice, and the schooners did not appear in any numbers, and as the result when the St. Lawrence cleared, they at once went to work filling there contracts for shipment up the St. Lawrence with as much despatch as possible. It must be remembered that as the result of the operation of these mines our people enjoyed good markets and steady employment, but the mines could not be operated if the company were prevented from filling their contracts.
Further on he says:
There had been accusations made against this particular company, but he maintained they were not well founded. He knew how this crusade started, and he could give some explanation of the motives behind it, but he would omit that for the present. Referring to the matter of the refusal of the company to supply a schooner with a barrel of coal-
Which alleged charge was referred to by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. A. Martin) this afternoon. The speaker said:
-he had investigated that, and the manager explained that he considered the request a joke. He was explaining the matter to the captains and trying to show them how impossible dt was for him at that time to do any better than lie was doing. He was up against a large contract that he was bound to fulfil or pay the penalty. If he had any choice in the matter he, would prefer the market in the maritime provinces, for one reason because the prices were better and it was in the interests of the company to sell as .much coal in the maritime provinces as possible, but the contracts for delivery up the St. Lawrence were necessary to keep the mine in operation and they had to be filled.
Now, I think that statement is a clear explanation on beliaif of the Inverness Coal and Railway Company, which seems to have been the only colliery complained of dur-Mr. A. K. MACLEAN.
ing tlie last season. Since this matter has been brought to the attention of tne Nova Scotia legislature, the only body authorized or competent to deal with it, I think we had better leave it with them, and because it is a matter with which this House has nothing to do either one way or the other.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speechtext: This question was brought some time ago to the attention of the department. I believe it was in the beginning of February that complaints reached the department to the effect that sailing vessels were discriminated against in loading coal at the collieries. At first we thought it was not possible for us to deal with this question except in cases where the wharfs or piers at which these vessels were loading, were under the control of the department. I caused some inquiries to be made from one of the complainants, who informed the department that the piers where they had been delayed belonged to the Dominion Coal Company, the Nova Scotia Steel Company, and also the Inverness Coal Company and the Acadian Coal Company at Plctou. He did not give, however, a statement of the dates when me delays occurred, he only mentioned those collieries as being those at which some delays occurred, without giving those other particulars. I thought it proper to communicate with our agent in Halifax, Mr. Parsons, in order to ascertain the nature of the complaints and whether it was possible to do anything in the matter. I received an answer from Mr. Parsons to the effect that these piers were all private property, that they were in no sense under the control of this government. If these piers at which sailing vessels were calling were government property, of course we might adopt some regulation that would meet the situation. But they all belong to the coal companies, and consequently the owners can do as they like. Now my hon. friend wants this government to regulate the way in which these mine owners shall sell and deliver their coal. That would be a very serious step to take; I do not know whether my hon. friend has given the matter all the consideration it deserves, I suppose he has done so. But once we undertake to interfere with the civil rights of any citizen in this country under the pretext of regulating trade, we enter upon a very serious undertaking. A citizen of the hon. gentleman's province is raising wheat, or oats, or potatoes, and he is certainly free to sell his produce in any way he likes; and what would my hon. friend think if this government were to frame a law by which a citizen of that province was obliged to deliver his grain or vegetables in such manner as this government thought best?
Does not this government undertake to regulate trade in canned meats, for instance hogs and pork?

It is true that we are regulating the sale of these things, we are regulating what should constitute the weight of a bushel of corn, or a bushel of potatoes, and what shall constitute a ton of coal. But what would he think of a law by which farmers were obliged to deliver their oats or potatoes in the quantity or to the person designated by this government. I am afraid that would be a dangerous step to take.

Is it not a fact that at Fort William and Port Arthur where the Canadian Pacific Railway and other private companies have elevators, the steamers have the privilege of loading in their regular turn, under a regulation of this government?
Tnose harbours are public property.
Are not the elevators public property?
No, the elevators are not public property.
Has not the Governor in Council power to regulate the way in which business is done at these harbours?

Where it is a public harbour or a public wharf well and good ; we have the right to interfere and to see that every one is treated in the same way, that vessels can load or unload in their turn, but tyhere it is a private property, as is the case here, it is another matter.
Are the Canadian Pacific Railway elevators private elevators ?

I think so, but they are in a public harbour. Take the case of these private wharfs, my hon. friend wants to force these collieries by legislation, to deliver coal to anybody who will go to one of their wharfs.
In their turn.
Not only in their turn, but absolutely. Suppose my hon. friend were the owner of a vessel there and they would not do any business with him, how could he force them to ?

They are there to do business with any person who pays the price of the coal. If he pays the price of the coal the government, as I read the Act, have the power to make regulations in regard to this as they have made them in regard to it at Montreal and some other points. If they have done it at these other points then I claim it is right they should do so here.

I am only pointing out the difficulties that are in the way. Suppose my hon. friend is a farmer, and a merchant comes to him and says : I want to purchase five bushels of oats or potatoes. My hon. friend would say :	No, I do not
want to sell five bushels ; I want to sell a larger quantity.

It is not a case at all of refusing to sell. They advertise to sell and they are ready to sell, but they say : We are ready to sell to you but we will keep your vessels here until some other vessels which have come after you are loaded.

That is not the point that I intended to make. Perhaps, when I have made it, the hon. gentleman will see the serious difficulties that are in the way. I do not say that I do not sympathize with the situation made to these smaller vessels, but I am trying to point out some of the difficulties. Returning to this illustration that I was going to give about the oats and potatoes,	suppose that a merchant comes to my hon. friend and says : I want to purchase five bushels of potatoes, and my hon. friend says :	No, I want to sell 100 bushels, or
200 busheis, or 1,000 bushels ; my hon. friend would be perfectly right in saying that. Potatoes and oats are just as much a necessity of life as coal is. Well then, my hon. friend sees the difficulties there are in the way of trying to force a private company to do business with a certain class of people in the way in which the government and parliament would like to have them do it. I am simply pointing out that difficulty. This is a question of property and civil rights. I think that the question has been dealt with in a proper manner by my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Maclean) and that, as he has pointed out, this is a question to be dealt with, not by this parliament, but by the province. The question is in the hands of the province. If it had been possible for us to have dealt with that question, if it had been a public wharf, I would have dealt with it immediately. When the correspondence is brought down my hon. friend will see that I took steps immediately to ascertain whether these were public wharfs or not. I wrote to the agent in Halifax in order to find out the situation and he says in his report that the situation which at present exists has existed for thirty years. Now, coming to the question which has been raised by the hon. member for Queen's, as to why we should not give the port wardens authority in the matter, I think that perhaps he has not given to that question the consideration which it deserves. Did I understand my hon. friend to say that we should pass regulations giving to the port wardens authority in the matter ?

I said that we have given authority to the port wardens at certain large ports, such as Quebec, Montreal, St. John and Halifax, and if we have done so at these ports I do not see why we should not give the same authority to the port wardens at other ports. The question I raised



has not been answered by the minister because he refers to these as private wharves. I referred him to several private elevators where they are subjected to rules and regulations which compel them to permit the loading of vessels in turn and if such a regulation applies to elevators and if the Governor in Council has power to make such regulations I do not see why the government could not do the same with reference to vessels at these coal loading ports.

As to this question of the port wardens, I see by section 875 of the Shipping Act, defining the duties and powers of port wardens, that the business which they have to perform does not at all relate to the point which my hon. friend wants to make :
The port wardens shall, at the request of any person interested proceed in person on board of any vessel for the purpose of examining the condition and stowage of her cargo, and if there are any goods damaged on board of snch vessel, he shall enquire, examine and ascertain the cause of such damage and make a memoranchim thereof, and enter the same in full on the books of his office.
If my hon. friend reads the definition of the duties and powers of port wardens, in this Act, he will find that the duties of port wardens have absolutely nothing to do with the placing and loading of vessels in a harbour. All they have to do is to see that a vessel is properly loaded.

Does the minister pretend to tell me that the harbour master or port warden has not the power to say where a vessel shall lie in the harbour, what wharf she shall lie at or what position she shall take ?

My hon. friend was referring to the port wardens. I am trying to show him that the duties of the port warden, under the Act, do not cover the point -which he was trying to make. His duties are absolutely different.
The minister is not answering iny question.

I am going to answer it. My hon. friend has been interrupting me and I am trying to make my points as quickly as possible, but, unfortunately, he goes faster than I do. He must see that the duties of the port warden have absolutely nothing to do with the question of *whether we can force mine owners to load a sailing vessel or to discriminate between a sailing vessel and a steam vessel. As to the harbour masters, while they have the right to place vessels at public wharfs I do not think they have any jurisdiction over wharfs which are owned by private parties.
They have the right to regulate any wharf whether it is public or private.
I think my hon. friend is mistaken.
I am not mistaken because I have had experience with it as a lawyer and have had cases. They have the power to regulate a private wharf.

My hon. friend says he has experience in the matter and I do not say he is wrong, but I always understood that it was only at public wharfs the harbour master has the right to determine the berthing of vessels. For instance, at Montreal harbour the harbour master there has a right to locate a vessel, but have we the right to say to the owner of a private wharf that a sailing vessel shall be loaded at such an hour and a steam vessel at such another hour ? I do not think so.

The. hon. minister is begging the question. I never said that. I said that under the regulations passed by the Marine and Fisheries Department the harbour master had the power to regulate how a vessel shall conduct itself at any pier whether it is private or public.

As to our constitutional right to deal with this question I fear it would be a serious step for us to undertake to regulate when and to whom a person shall sell his coal. I understand that the legislature of Nova Scotia is dealing with the question and I think it is much better to leave it in the hands of the provincial legislature than for this parliament to interfere, as it is a question of property and civil rights which falls under section 92 of the British North America Act rather than under section 91. I understand that some hon. members of the House have made representations to the coal companies about the matter and that is perhaps the proper way to deal with the question. In recent years there has been a great development of the coal trade. I remember that some years ago the industrial establishments of Montreal were using United States coal, but now I think that nearly all of it comes from Nova Scotia, and I should be sorry to see anything done which would restrict this trade and give opportunities to the Americans to take it up again. It is our duty to make every effort to encourage interprovincial trade and I am sure that the province of Prince Edward Island would be the first to manifest its desire in that direction. I have had the opportunity of discussing this matter with some of the coal mine owners and they have informed me that the conditions of the coal trade last year were exceptional and that there would be no grievance this year. In view of all this I think the complaint of the hon. gentleman is hardly a live grievance to-day.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday last my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) directed the attention of the House to the fact that a large number of Are extinguishers had been purchased by this government during the past few years. Later on in the afternoon the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries took up the question in a personal explanation, and during the course of his remarks, which will be found on page 7901 of ' Hansard,' stated :
I sent over to the department for the file and I find that on July 20, 1906, Mr. Perreault applied to the depatment to sell some fire extinguishers, and on July 27, 1906, the letter which I have just quoted was written and signed by the deputy minister.
Further on in the discussion, after the hon. minister had quoted from the original file, Mr. Blain said :
246i
I suppose the hon. gentleman would have no objection to lay the file on the table?
Some further discussion took place which ended in the hon. minister laying the file on the table of the House. Immediately the House adjourned for six o'clock, and I applied to the clerk for the file, which was courteously given to me, with the understanding that I would return it before the close of that evening's sitting, so that the clerk, having the custody of the file, could lock it up in his vault. My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster), on the following morning, Saturday morning, applied for the file, and was told that immediately after it had been returned to the clerk on Friday night, the minister had come for it and had taken it away. This morning I made application to the clerk for the file, and the clerk immediately corresponded with the minister, with the result that at three o'clock, when the House opened, the file was not here. It is only fair to say that the minister sent for me and said that he was quite willing to have the whole file copied and the copies laid on the table of the House. I said to my hon. friend that was not the point, but that the point was as to whether the hon. minister, having quoted extensively from an original file, and having laid that file upon the table of the House, and while it was in the custody of the clerk for the use of members, would have the right to make application to the clerk and take the file away, and refuse to return it to the custody of the clerk. If any minister of the Crown has the right to do that, it will be impossible for the members of this House on the opposition side to make any thorough examination of any file or of any great public question. The hon. minister had no right to take that file away otherwise than to use it as any other member of the House would use it, and with the distinct understanding that he would return it to the clerk so that other members of the House could have an opportunity to use it. I cannot understand why the hon. minister should not have been quite willing to leave the file with the clerk. Is there anything in it which the members of this House should not see? We have had a good deal of discussion recently in regard to original documents. We have been told that copies were as valuable for the discussion of public questions as originals; but we have found that that was not the case, because when the originals were brought down, after a contest in the House, they told a very different story from the copies. As to whether the originals will tell a different story from the copies in this ease, I do not know, because I have had no opportunity as a private member to go fully over the file. I scanned it in the short time at my disposal. The file is a rather large one. The hon. minister has the original before him now. I take the ground that the minister has no

more right to these public documents after they are placed on the table of the House and in the custody of the clerk than any other member of this House.

Will the hon. member allow me a question ? Suppose some business were to be transacted in the department in connection with some matters to which a part of this file referred, would not the minister be justified in calling that file back in order that he might transact that business?

I want to be courteous towards my hon. friend. There is a way of getting the file. There certainly is the way laid down by my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior a few days ago in a discussion on this important question. In answer to my hon. friend I may say that if any great public investigation were going on, and the hon. minister required the original file, he could bring the matter up in the House, and I am sure that the House would unanimously say that the original documents should be used. But to say that after a document has been laid on the table of the House, any minister of the Crown has the right to go to the clerk and take it away, and to suggest that he would put a copy in place of it, is something which I am sure neither this House nor the people of Canada will tolerate. I have before me ' Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure,' which at page 461 says :
It has been laid down by the highest authorities that when a minister of the Crown quotes a public document in the House, and founds upon it an argument or an assertion, that document, if called for, ought to be produced. But it is allowable to repeat to the House information which is contained in a private communication. When such private papers are quoted in the House there is no rule requiring them to be laid on the table. The rule respecting the production of public papers, quoted by a minister of the Crown, is necessary to give the House the same information he possesses and enable it to come to a correct conclusion on a question.
That is the opinion of a gentleman whose authority of course is accepted by the right hon. the First Minister aud every member of this House. I do not wish to detaiD the House at any length. This fire extinguisher question has created considerable excitement among the people. They are very much aroused at the idea that any man should sell fire extinguishers in so large a number to this government simply to be stored away in the city of Montreal. And, according to the correspondence, while they were stored away in Montreal, the department purchased other fire extinguishers. Mr. Charles Patton sold 600 at $15 each during 1903-4 and was paid $9,000. In 1907-8 he sold 100 more to this government at $15 each and received $1,500. And a new firm, styled Patton & Crowe, sold 95 more at $15 a piece, and were paid $1,425. As to whe-Mr. BLAIN.
ther the Patton of Patton & Crowe is the original Charles Patton I do not know. 1 have had no opportunity of examining the file to ascertain if that be the case, but 1 presume that he is. However on that point I may be wrong. What explanation can the minister give why he should have stepped in and taken away the original documents, and then, in answer to myself, promise to bring down in a day or two, when the opportunity presented itself, copies of these, original documents. I presume he will do so, but I repeat I am not aware that any minister of the Crown has the right, after having laid a file on the table and after having quoted extensively from it, to go to the clerk aud take it away from him and say that he will replace it by copies. Let me just give one extract from the file, which will no doubt create some interest among members of this House and the people in general, as a sample of what the file held:
Ottawa, July 8, 1903.
Copy of an agreement.
Por and in consideration of $1 and other good and valuable considerations, receipt acknowledged, the undersigned hereby agrees to and binds himself to pay C. S. Cameron the sum of $2,000 in the following manner: $1,000 on receipt of an order from the Department of Marine and Fisheries for 500 of my Star Glass-lined Chemical Fire Extinguishers, and a further $1,000 three months after date of the receipt of said order and pro rata thereof for -any order.

So we have reached the point in connection with these fire extinguishers when Mr. Patton is able, out of bis payment of $15 for fire extinguishers to pay Mr. Cameron the handsome sum of $4 apiece for securing an order from the government.
To whom does he agree to pay it?

To C. S. Cameron.
The above is a true copy of the agreement between Charles Patton and the undersigned.

What happened ? Did Mr. Patton sell any fire extinguishers to the government ? Of course he did. An order was secured and $9,000 was paid. That is what the original document told us. I do not wish to take up the time of the House quoting any further extracts or copies from the letters on the file; but I say that, in fairness to the House and the country, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries should place with the clerk the original file, so that every member of this House may have the opportunity of looking into it. It is no excuse for him to say he will give a copy. He might have had the right in the discussion to say that he would only lay on the table the letters he quoted-on which point I offer no opinion-but of his own free will

he placed the whole file on the table and as I understood, put it In charge o£ the clerk of the House. Under the circumstances, I do not see that he has the right to take away again that file from the clerk. If after having laid the file on the table, he made application to the clerk before any other member had the opportunity of doing so, and carried away the file, he would thus deprive any other member of the right to look at it at all. After we have had so much discussion over the retention of public documents by this government, over their secrecy, and over their efforts to keep back original documents from the inspection of the House, and in view of the suspicions that have been aroused among hon. members on this side and the people owing to that secretive method, one would hardly expect that the hon. minister would think for a moment of keeping away this original file from inspection by the members of this House ; and I submit we have the right to expect that he will stand up in his place and agree to return the original file to the clerk, which he laid on the table in the discussion on Friday last.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the House had better not assume without consideration that the practice in the one case is the same as in the other. If a minister of the Crown quotes from a public document, and

a demand is made it is necessary to produce it and lay it upon tlie table of tbe House for tbe purpose of inspection and for use in tbe debate which is then in progress. But, the House is not to assume that the rule in that case is the same as when a document is laid before the House by order of the House on motion. I am not now laying down any particular rule except to ask that the House may not assume that the rule is the same in the one case as in the other. In the ordinary course of laying documents upon the table of the House there must be some parliamentary authority for that purpose and that is expressly laid down in Bourinot's work-from which the hon. member for Peel has quoted-at page 357 :
No documents can be regularly laid before the House unless in pursuance of some parliamentary authority.
Hon. members can easily see what would happen if a different rule were to be assumed and followed. In the midst of a debate a minister might quote from a public document, and at the request of a member produce it and lay it on the table of the House, as he would be obliged to do, having quoted from it or having based an argument upon its contents. But without an order of the House it would not be regularly laid on the table of the House; and it would hardly be a regular proceeding to interrupt a debate for the purpose of moving that an order of the House be made to lay it on the table. Without desiring to lay down any hard and fast rule at the moment, but only gathering from the discussion as it has been going on that it was assumed that the proceeding would necessarily be the same in the one case as in the other, I thought I should call -the attention of the House to this distinction. The chair would assume that in this instance the proceeding would be that the minister, when called on to produce the document, should produce it for the purpose of inspection, though it would not go formally into the possession of the House and become a part of its archives, as in the case of a document laid on the table, by motion; and that will appear from the fact that in the present instance there is no record in the Votes and Proceedings of the matter, as is customary in the case of documents laid on the table of the House by order of the House itself,

Well, Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend expressed to me this afternoon his desire to see the whole file, and I have no objection to letting him see it. If he comes to my department I shall be glad to show it to him. and as soon as the copies are made-I am having it copied-if he wants a copy brought to the House, I will bring it. I shall be glad to have all the facts contained in this file made known; I have nothing to hide, and have no intention
to hide anything. In conclusion, I think the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) will bear testimony to my strong desire to meet his wishes in every respect. He knows that I showed him all the papers in connection with this matter, and that he expressed to me his satisfaction that the documents had been signed as I stated. He found, however, that it would be advisable for him to go over the whole file and see if he could not discover something else. He seems to have discovered a document which shows that a man wanted to sell some fire extinguishers to the department and did not succeed. So that it is shown conclusively that there is absolutely nothing against the department, and I am sorry that we have lost so much time on this incident.
However much time has been occupied in the discussion of this question, I think it is so important that nobody will object to time being so occupied.
If my hon. friend will permit me to interrupt him, I would like the minister to put this file on the table so that I may inspect it. He has been quoting from it and making his case anew.
I will do so, subject to inspection.

The hon. gentleman, starting out with what I suppose he thought was an answer to the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain), immediately began as a diversion with an attack on the hon. mem-mer for Leeds (Mr. Taylor). He sought to represent that the hon. member for Leeds had misstated the facts with regard to letters sent b.v the hon. gentleman's department, that is by the hon. gentleman, to persons having dealings with the department. Now, I have before me ' Hansard ' unrevised of May 1, page 7877, and we will there see exactly what the hon. member for Leeds said, and precisely what line the hon. minister took in answer to him. The hon. member for Leeds said :
Let mo draw attention to a letter which he
,p, minister) wrote, following the lines on which his predecessor had worked. It will be found in the report of the commissioners on page 79. It was written by the minister to Mr. Gregory at Quebec, and was dated July 27, 1906.
I do not propose to occupy the time of the House in entering into the question that was raised by that correspondence. Tbe sole question here is, as to whether the member for Leeds quoted honestly and properly as a member of this House, and whether the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries was correct in his repudiation of the letter, because it amounted to that. If he did not repudiate the letter or his responsibility for the letter, there was no need for his intervention. We all know In these days that a business man does not sign one

letter out of twenty with his own hand, and yet they are all his letters. We all know that a business man writes hundreds of letters in a day; but he does not sign_ them all; he dictates them, and they are issued by his authority, and he is responsible for them. A lawyer will write hundreds of letters in the course of a day; he does not sign one of them, but they are all his letters. Above all the head of a department, with hundreds of letters going out everyday, would never undertake to sign all the letters; he makes no pretension of doing so; and yet every letter is his letter, and he is responsible for it. Now, the hon. member for Leeds said that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries wrote a letter on a certain subject, and he went on to say :
If Mr. Gregory could get a letter that indicated more clearly to him that he should purchase a number of these fire extinguishers than that letter written by the minister on the 27th of July, 1908. I do not know what better authority he could have. This is the letter from the minister.
Then the hon. gentleman went on to quote the letter. Now, let us see how this ingenuous, straightforward minister dealt with that question:

Where does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) find that I ever

Did he say wrote ?
-signed such a letter?
Was that an equivocation ? I would say it was. Then the hon. member for Leeds went on:	.
If the minister will bring down the files, I will point out the letter.

The hon. gentleman says he has seen the file and knows there is a letter written by me. Does he assert that I have signed it?
Signed it. That is the point which this minister of the Crown is making-the minister of a great department, who knows that he seldom ever signs a letter unless it be one marked ' private and confidential,' What did the minister mean this House to understand by that? Did he mean that the House was to understand merely that it was signed by his authority but not by himself? No, it was intended to convey the idea that he repudiated the letter entirely; but he used the word 'signed' to convey the impression that he had not written the letter. The hon. member for Leeds went on to say :
The commissioners have gone through the file and have given the House their report stating what they found.
The minister then replied:
There is no statement that I signed the letter.
Note how he sticks to that word ' signed.' Did he not know the distinction between Mr. BARKER.
putting his own name with his own hand to a letter and the writing of a letter by his authority? Then the member for Leeds went on:
If the minister will produce the letter, no doubt his signature will he found at the bottom of it.
Hear, hear. What does that mean?
It did not mean that the signature was -written by the hon. gentleman himself. The hon. minister is again resorting to a quibble.
I do not know what a quibble is then.

Let me tell him. Did any man ever find a business firm, a railway company, a large corporation, a law firm or anybody repudiating their letters because a member of the firm did not put his own signature to it? The letter was signed by the minister's authority and he knew it.

But the hon. member for Leeds said that if I would produce the letter, no doubt my signature would be found at the bottom of it.
Mr. BARKER, It was signed by the minister's authority, just as 90 per cent of the letters to-day are written and signed. No honourable man, no honourable firm, no honourable corporation, repudiates its signature when put to a document by its authority. The hon. minister goes on. He sticks to his point. He knows the distinction between a letter written by authority and a letter signed by the minister himself, hut he goes on and asks again:
Does the hon. gentleman assert that I signed that letter?
He sticks to that quibble carefully, absolutely, knowing the distinction. The hon. member for Leeds says :
I am making no assertion. The hon. minister appointed a royal commission, and I am quoting what the royal commission said.
The miniser then replies.
No, that does not say that I signed the letter. Does the hon. gentleman say that I signed it ?
Again sticking to the quibble-a little trumpery distinction between the man writing his signature himself and that signature and letter being written by his authority. Then he says again :
The hon. member for Leeds has stated that I signed that letter.
The hon. member for Leeds replies:
I did not make that statement.
Then we have the minister again saying:
I deny that I signed it.

Now the hon. minister in a certain sense says truthfully that he himself did not sign that letter, but did the use he made of that word ' sign ' from the beginning of this discussion to the end, convey the impression of truth? No honourable man in this Dominion will doubt that the hon. gentleman was seeking to convey a mis-statement to the country. He was trying to convey to the country the idea that he was not responsible for that letter by repeating that he never signed it, although it was signed by his authority. My hon. friend from Leeds went on to say:
I want to make my'speech. X am reading from the report of the royal commission.
What does the minister repeat?
The hon. gentleman said I had signed the letter.
He was holding him to the word 1 signed,' and he construed that word. The hon. member for Leeds repeated:
I say this is from the head of the department, from the minister, for further down there is one from the deputy and they quote his name.
The first, on page 78 and 79, he says was from the minister, but the second letter purported to come from the deputy. From whom did the first purport to come? From the hon. the minister, and it was signed by his authority; yet again, after all this was asserted and re-asserted before the House, the minister gets up again and asks: Does the hon. gentleman assert that I signed it? What a pitiful, wretched, miserable attempt at an explanation. Why, Mr. Speaker, such conduct is worthy alone of a political police court shyster. It was a mere sham, a pretense, and the hon. minister knew it

an absolute sham and pretense intended to convey to this country that that was an unauthorized letter and that the minister was not responsible, when the absolute contrary was the fact. I now come to the question raised by my hon. feirnd from Peel. He asked why he, a member of this House, had not every right which the minister had. Inside these four walls of this chamber what distinction is there, as a matter of right, between he member for Peel and the minister? Have the people of Britain been fighting for centuries for popular rights and are we now to be told that the Crown, through its minister, can claim rights the people do not enjoy? Is that to be the case to-day? Is It to be the case that a minister can take away from the clerk of the House of Commons certain public papers and that that clerk cannot give these papers to the humblest member of this House? Is that what we are to be told by a Liberal government under the aegis of the right hon. gentleman? Are we to be told that a member of this House cannot see an original paper, which Is in the possession of the
clerk of this House, but that a minister of the Crown-or in other words the Crown itself-can take that paper and say to the House: Oh, you can have a copy but you shall not see the original. Is that the position to-day? Will the hon. gentleman contend for a moment that a minister can take from the custody of the clerk of the House papers which that clerk has in his possession -original papers-and prevent other members having access to them? Has a minister the right to say to the members of this House: You shall no see the original paper, but if you like I will, by my grace and courtesy, give you a copy ? Has it come to that point in a British parliament that we are to be told that that is the sum of our rights-that an hon. gentleman, a minister, can stand up and say: Oh, there is a commission sitting, and I took these papers because that commission might want them. Why, the hon. minister does not dare tell the House that he took these papers for the commission. Did he give them to the commission? Did the commission ask for them? A member of the House wanted to see them, but the minister had taken them from the possession of the clerk. Why, we had a week's discussion not long since upon papers put into the possession of the House, and we were then told by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver)-and I think by the right hon. gentleman himself and other ministers-that they could not allow original papers to go into possession of the clerk because they oculd not be got back again by the department, for the use of the department, without an order of the House. When, however, it suits the minister, when it is convenient, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries can go to the clerk and take the papers out of his possession without our order. That is the point my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) has raised; and the hon. minister has not uttered one solitary excuse, not a word in answer to the charge made against him that he took papers out of the possession of the clerk of this House and thus prevented other members of this House having access to them.

The hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) has seen fit to refer to a discussion which took place here on Friday night last and to repudiate altogether a certain letter that was written to Mr. Gregory, agent of the department at Quebec, on the 27th July, 11309. Let me quote that letter again. it is dated July 27th, 1906:
I have to inform you that if you consider that chemical fire extinguishers are necessary on board the vessels of the Quebec agency, you are to purchase them from P. E. Perreault, 312 St. John street, Quebec. Mr. Perreault has been advised to call upon you in connection with this matter.
That was a letter from the department of which the hon. minister is the head, author-

izing Mr. Gregory, if lie required any fire extinguishers, to purchase them from Mr. Perreault and stating that Mr. Perreault had been written to.
Then, he quotes here to-night a letter of his own, dated March 12, 1907, and saying that they did not want any fire extinguishers. But before this, the letter of July 27, 1906, had been acted upon and the department had been loaded up with these fire extinguishers. If the minister will turn to the Auditor General's Report, he will find a record, page P-19, showing that Mr. Perreault had sent in an account for eight of these fire extinguishers at $112. Then, at page P-23, 8; page P-36, 8; page P-57, 16 ; page P-100, 8 ; page P-104, 4 -altogether 52 fire extinguishers bought on the strength of that letter of July 27, 1906, and before the minister wrote his further letter. Then, there was the letter written to Mr. Gregory to know by what authority he purchased these articles, and Mr. Gregory wrote back that he had purchased them ' by authority of your letter of July 27.' If the minister repudiated that letter of July 27, why did he pay the accounts ? Why did he not repudiate the accounts also ? But the accounts were certified correct, and the Auditor General paid the money. And now the minister gets up and tells us that when the matter came to his notice he wrote this letter of March 12, 1907. But was not this purchase authorized by him ? When I speak of the minister, I speak of the department.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) is getting more cautious.

I am not getting more cautious. Has a Minister of the Crown no responsibility ? Why, let the president of a bank say of any act of the bank: This was done by one of the clerks ; let the president of any mercantile company say : I did not authorize this, it was the act of one of the clerks or superintendents, and what would be thought of him ? Why, we might as well have a sack of wool in the minister's	chair if	that	is all the responsibility he	is going to	assume.	Wemight as well	have a	man	of putty	as aman if he is	allowed	to repudiate	what
his deputy does. He kept his deputy there even after this came to his knowledge. I am surprised at the minister saying that he did not write this letter of July 27, 1906. I am satisfied that there is not a deputy in any department who would take it upon himself to write such a letter, for it is a political letter. It simply says : If you consider that chemical fire extinguishers are necessary, you are to purchase them from my friend P. E. Perreault, who has been advised to call upon you. And, of course, the man thus instructed did buy them to the amount of $792. And the minister tells us in his speech that the late government purchased two Babcock Mr. TAYLOR.
engines. Why a Babcock is worth a dozen of these. Everybody knows what a Babcock is. But these little glass-lined things that were sold at $14 to the Department of Marine and $15 to the Department of Public Works are not in the same class at all. They were sold to the Public Works Department through my friend Le-mieux, agent for the firm of Patton & Crowe, which was really the firm of Patton & Grant, with no Crowe in it at all. I know something about it, and I received a letter from my friend Lemieux, published in the ' Free Press,' saying that his * honoured name ' should not be dragged in. His ' honoured name ! ' I will not refer further to this matter, though, if he provokes me much more I will. And the idea of the minister saying that I ran away and was not here when he spoke in answer to me. I never ran away from anybody in this House. There is enough Irish in me that if I am knocked down I will get up and fight again. No minister can bluff me, as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries tries to do. And the minister pleads the baby act. He goes to the province of Quebec and says:	It is because I am
