a Frenchman that they attack me.' No one but a baby would make such a plea. And hear him yelping here to-night, and read the speech he made on Friday night. I am surprised that any man professing to be a statesman should resort to such conduct in this House. I will say no more about this at present, but I wanted to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that the letter written on July 27, is borne out by the facts in the Auditor General's return, showing that the minister himself purchased 792 of these machines after he wrote that letter to Perreault, and before he wrote the other letter in March, 1907. I say he was responsible for the purchase. No matter who did it in his department or in his agency, it was done with his' consent and his knowledge.
Does the hon. member menu to say that this purchase was made on my authority and with my consent ?

I say that this letter was never written by the deputy without his having been authorized to do so by the minister. If a deputy of mine would do it, he would not write a second one. The facts are there. Gregory went on and bought these machines knowing that that letter was authorized by the minister. Besides, Gregory had a private letter, because this letter says, Gregory had been advised of the fact. There is no jury in the world who would acquit the minister and convict the deputy on a statement such as his.

The matter that has occupied the time of the House to-night, and that some might say has been wasted, might well not have

been wasted it the Minister ot Marine and Fisheries had been a little more reasonable. He knows that the Prime Minister said that he was anxious to see the truth and the whole truth spread before the House. Why then should he object to the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) and myself looking over that hie ? If there was nothing to conceal why did the minister take up the time of the House and cause all- this hubbub by taking away the papers which the member for Peel thought he should not have done ? Why could he not this morning have given this file to the member for Peel ?-and I venture to say that in three or four hours the member for Peel would have got all he wanted out of them, and could have handed back the papers to the clerk, and nobody would have suffered from any delay. It seems to me to be childish for the minister to try to avoid showing these papers for a few hours on the pretext that the commission is sitting and his department is preparing papers. If we are to believe the minister that all the contracts are being prepared to go before this commission, does he mean. to say that any great delay would have occurred, that anything would have been broken, if for a few hours to-day he had handed these papers over to my hon. friend from Peel and allowed him to look at them ?

At noon to-day while I was sitting in a committee of this House, I received a letter from the clerk asking me whether I had the file in my possession. I was busy until one o'clock or a quarter past one, in the committee, and as soon as I came into the House at three o'clock, I showed the file to my hon. friend.

I came up about half-past eight or nine o'clock on Saturday morning and went to the clerk's office thinking I would find the file there, and if I could have seen it for an hour or two, I would have been satisfied. The minister could have avoided all this row if he had furnished us at the proper time the file for inspection. What is meant by inspection ? It is sufficient when a minister quotes from a large file, that he shall lay it on the table and then take it off the next minute, or after five minutes, or after half an hour ? Inspection means that the member who wishes to see it shall have reasonable time to look over it and familiarize himself with it. The minister comes to-day and makes the matter still worse by taking hold of that file and quoting from still other documents that are in it. For what purpose is the file requested to be placed on the table ? That you may see some letter that he quotes ? Of course not. What we are discussing is the question of fire extinguishers, this whole file refers to fire extinguishers, and you are not at all in possession of the information when you simply see one, or two, or three
letters that the minister chooses to read. What you have a right to do is to look over the file to see whether there is anything that sheds light, and may be gives a contradiction to the gloss the minister himself puts upon it. Is it sufficient to take up a scientific work and read ten lines out of a book of two hundred pages, and then, when any one questions whether you have correctly stated the essence of the book, for you to hand it over to him and say, Well, you can read these ten lines ; there they are. That does not satisfy the conditions at all. What he needs to do is to take the sense of the whole document, and to do so he must examine the whole file. After what the House has heard to night it has come to the. conclusion that my hon. friend from Peel struck a mare's nest when he read something about an agreement between Mr. Cameron and Mr. Patton with reference to ROD fire extinguishers, and the minister thought he had set it all at rest by declaring that that order was cancelled. I think there is a little more history in this affair than the minister has shown us. I have only had three or four minutes to look over the file, but I find in it a little bit of his tory that will put a different gloss upon the matter. I find that on December 14, 1901, Mr. A. W. Fraser interests himself in this matter of fire extinguishers. Is there anything in which Mr. Fraser has not interested himself in connection with all these departments? Here we find him and there we find him. Here is what he says :
Hon. James Sutherland,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-I am informed that many of the lighthouses under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries are not supplied with any appliances for extinguishing fire, should such occur, and that some of the officers have under consideration the fire extinguisher being sold by Mr. Patton of this city.
That is Ottawa.
As I mentioned to you the other day, Mr. Patton has been a very good friend of the Liberal party

And here is where it comes in.

and a liberal one.
Does that mean liberal in the way of political or party doctrine? I will read it again.
Mr. Patton has been a very good friend of the Liberal party and a liberal one.
I take it that that is to be interpreted not in the party sense but in the financial sense. Here is the old principle coming out again-you scratch my back and I will scratch yours; you put money into my pocket and I will give you a little money back for yourself; you give me patronage and I will whack up when It comes to the election.

Therefore I hope you will be able to give him an order

Because he is a very good Liberal and a very liberal Liberal.
Therefore I hope you will he able to give him an order for at least 100 of these extinguishers. Mr. Patton is quite willing to wait for payment until after your estimates have been voted providing he receives an order, as he can arrange the matter in the meantime.
There is again the old virus. There is again the well known principle which actuates this government. It does not make any difference as to parliamentary appropriations. You give the order, sign the contract, make everything fast as far as the government is concerned, and by and by when you come to the House you will get your money because your men will stand behind you. Mr. Fraser knew that.
I have just learned also that some time ago he supplied some of these extinguishers to the Public Works department and that the order was given during the time Mr. Mulock was acting minister of the department. After you have looked into the matter will you kindly let me know what prospects there are of doing anything for him?
Yours sincerely,

So much for that, away back in 1901. And then it goes on until we come to the incident that was mentioned by my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) in which it appears that Mr. Patton and Mr. Cameron joined forces. Mr. Cameron was to get an order for 500 or 600 extinguishers and he was to get $2,000 paid to him for getting the order. Now, Mr. Speaker, it is well to inquire who loses by the payment of that $2,000. We know who would pay the $2,000 for getting a proper person to sell to the department. We know who would make the loss. It is so much more that the country has to pay for this go-between. And, who was the go-between? So, that went on and an order was absolutely given to Mr. Cameron. Here it is :
March 9, 1904.
I am to inform you that the department has made a careful examination of the Patton fire extinguisher, and considers that it is suited for the lighthouse service of Canada inasmuch as it will not freeze and being glass lined will not corrode, the acid being hermetically sealed in a bulb.
The department will require six hundred of these extinguishers with materials sufficient to recharge twice, at a cost of $15 each which I am to request you to supply, it being understood that they are to be furnished ready to act and boxed as per sample. No payment to be made until after July 1.
I am sir, your obedient servant.
(Sgd.) F. GOURDEAU,
Deputy Minister Marine and Fisheries. C. S. Cameron, Esq.,
Manager Patton Fire Extinguisher, Ottawa.

That was the letter issued by the department. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries says : Oh. that does not amount to anything, the minister never signed it. But, the department or the minister, who is the head of the department, is absolutely responsible for the order. Well, but the minister says, that order was caught up on the way. That is true ; It was caught up on the way. Shortly after that we have a letter from Charles Patton to one O. E. Culbert, solicitor for the Montreal Fire Extinguisher Company :
Dear Sir,-I hereby agree that in consideration of your organizing a company in the province of Quebec to manufacture and sell my machines to give to such company the right to manufacture and sell my machines and I appoint such company as my attorney and agent in that behalf.
Yours truly, CHARLES PATTON.
That goes. Then we find on March 22, 1904, this very peculiar letter :
C. S. Cameron, Esq.,
54 Sparks street, Ottawa.
A departmental letter dated 9th March, instant, purporting to order from you some fire extinguishers which the department had decided to order from the Montreal Fire Extinguisher Company, on instructions received by me to that effect, through error, was addressed to you instead of Mr. O E. Culbert representing said company. As the error has come to my knowledge and might create some misunderstanding I hereby make you acquainted with the facts so that you may not consider said letter as an order.
Believe me, yours truly (Sgd.) R. PREFONTAINE.
The deputy minister was instructed to send out that letter and he did send out that letter to Mr. Cameron. Shortly afterwards there is the following letter :
Ottawa, April 16, 1901.
The Hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Dear Sir,-I' would like the order for fire extinguishers to be made out to Charles Patton and Mr. Cameron has agreed to this. As we are making our arrangements to-day I would be very greatly obliged if the order could issue this morning. With your permission I shall send a messenger for it.
Faithfuly yours,

Then there is this other letter:
April 14 1904.
The Hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge the receipt of the letter from your department dated March 28, 1894, cancelling the order from said department for 600" Patton fire extinguishers dated March 9, 1904, and I agree to the cancellation of the said order. I am also willing that an order should be issued to O. E. Culbert for the said fire extinguishers he having entered into an agreement with me

bearing even date .herewith in regard to the same.	,
Yours truly,

April 15, 1901.
To the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Ottawa.
Sir,-I am willing that the order for fire extinguishers should be made out to Charles Patton or to O. E. Culbert, and as these gentlemen would rather have it issued to Mr. Patton I would make it out in his name he having signed the agreement to me with Mr. Culbert.
Yours truly,
C.; S. CAMERON.
There Is an agreement, first signed by Mr. Culbert, and second, signed by Mr. Patton with Mr. Culbert. Mr. Cameron says:	I have made my agreement with
these gentlemen and you may send the order to them if you please. The agreement made between these gentlemen, is, as far as I have seen, not on the file. What was that agreement? It is plain enough to me, I think it is plain enough to any one, that by the change Cameron's interest has not been sacrificed, and that, although he did not get the contract himself, there is every probability that his interest has not been sacrificed but that it has been taken care of by these other gentlemen getting it and that the country has paid the amount of the remuneration received by the go-betweens. Well that order was absolutely issued; it was not only issued but here is an acknowledgement of it.
F. Gourdeau, Esq., Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge receipt of your favour of the 20th instant ordering from me 600 fire extinguishers. I shall fill the order at the earliest date possible. Thanking you for the same, I remain yours,
What is the date of that ?

April 25, 1904. Then we find that Wm. Alexander Cameron and Robert George Cameron doing business under the name of Cameron & Company give a power of attorney to a certain bank and that the bank notifies the department of the power of attorney being given authorizing the payment to the bank of any moneys which are coming on this contract, and so it goes on and on. What else there is I do not know because I have not had time to look into it. Now, I say that puts a different face upon this transaction to what it carried when the Minister of Marine read the partial correspondence. I say that if this laying on the table a document from which you quote is going to be any thing but a farce, you must not only lay the Simple quotation but you must lay the whole document upon the table and you must lay it sufficiently long for a person to look into 247
it and become acquainted with all its contents. It looks to me as if this is absolutely as much a document as if it were all printed and put within covers and laid upon the table of this House and used by any man in the House. That it is in manuscript does not prevent its being considered one document for it is the whole history of the fire extinguisher business, and you have got to go into this case as far as 1901 and maybe further in order to show the beginnings which afterwards resulted in this 600 extinguisher order with this very large amount of bonus or of commission which was paid. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, while I quite agree that there is a difference between this and a document coming down by an order of the House, yet it is the property of the House the moment it is put here and no man can take it away and keep another member from having it for a reasonable time to satisfy his own curiosity or desire for information. It seems to me that if there is any virtue at all in the rule which makes a minister put upon the table of the House a document from which he quotes, the virtue must be in it for the reason that it gives the other person to the argument a chance to test the argument, and test the conclusion which was come to by the first gentleman who uses it-the minister in this case. If that had been done there need be no row about it at all. It could have been done if the minister had conceded thBs paper to my friend (Mr. Blain) and if he wanted to take it back when no one else was using it and use it in his department I think that would not be going much beyond what was right. When it was asked again for the very purpose for which it was in the first place put upon the table of the House I think it would have been well for the minister courteously to have conceded and said : Yes, Mr. Blain, look this over and send it back.
That is what I have done. I told the hon. member for Peel that he could see the file as long as he liked.
Where could he see it ?
In my room this afternoon.
At three o'clock ?
Yes.

The minister has no right to dictate where a man is going to peruse these papers. When a paper is laid upon the table of the House the member who wishes to use it uses it where he thinks proper, takes his notes, and when he has done with it he puts it back. If these papers are left on the table of the House my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) would be able to satisfy himself without any very great length of time, and if it were necessary to have them back in the Department of Mar-

ine lie would be only too glad to let the minister have them when they were required. But it is pretty perilous to allow a minister any more than any other member to take a paper which was put upon the table of the House in accordance with the rules and allow the minister to come and take it away and refuse to give it back again. I think that is not courteous to the House and I do not believe it comes within -the rule of the House which if it means anything must mean that it gives reasonable time for a member to look into a document from which quotations have been made. With reference to the letters; looking at page 79 of the report I would have done exactly as my hon. friend from Leeds did. There are five letters referred to on that page, the first one is :
July 27, 1906.
I have -to inform you that if you consider that chemical fire extinguishers are necessary on board the vessels of the Quebec agency, you are to purchase them from P. E. Perreault, 312 St. John street, Quebec. Mr. P. has been advised to call upon you in connection with this matter.
Is there a copy of that advice on the file.

I think I saw that letter on the file.
Mr. iBRODBIJR. You had better quote it because the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) does not believe it yet.
That is not an assertion which comes very gracefully from my hon. friend. I think he had better treat his fellow members a little differently.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) did not seem to believe it.
To-night I noticed that the minister referred to my hon. friend from Leeds as ' that man ' and ' the man.' You might as well call him the hon. member for so and so.
Do you always remember these little courtesies ?
I am generally very courteous to the members of this House.
Sometimes.

I try to be. Then, under date October 8, 1906, Gregory writes about fire extinguishers bought from Perreault, and on October 12, there is another letter from the deputy. I would have done the same thing as my friend from Leeds did ; 1 would have thought that the first letter was a letter from the minister himself or written by the minister's authority and I could not have come to any other conclusion. The second letter shows it was from Gregory, the third letter shows it was a letter from the deputy, the next one shows Mr. FOSTER.
it is a letter from Gregory and the next one is a quotation from Gregory's letter. Maybe the fault was that the commissioner was not explicit enough or he would have said that that first letter was a letter from the deputy but on the face of it it appears to be a letter from the minister himself or written by authority of the minister. Anyway the contention is absolutely good that where orders are made in a case of this kind if they are made by the deputy minister they are made with the authority of the minister.

PATERSON1 (Minister of Customs). I do not profess to be an authority on this matter, but I wish to say a word as to how it strikes me in view of what Sir. Speaker has laid down, not as a ruling but in a general way. It does seem to me that what he says must commend itself to the good sense of the House. Complaint was made that a document which had been laid on the table had been taken away by the hon. gentleman who had laid it on the table.

If my hon. friend will allow me just there. I do submit to him that that would have no force in the argument at all. You might have an original paper brought down by the order of the House, and it might be lost; but that would be no argument that thereafter no original paper should be brought down. Now, this might be lost. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries is a lawyer, and I vflll venture to say that if any advocate would endeavour to prove before a court of law on the evidence which he has adduced tonight, that an original paper in the Markey case was lost by a member of the opposition, no one would depreciate that argument more quickly than the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries. The evidence does not form a perfect chain. Has he proved that the ' Hansard ' reporter put that original back again, after it was read by a member of the opposition, into the hands of the opposition ? He does not prove it; he assumes that it was done. But I myself have lost documents between my handing them over to the * Hansard ' and their not getting them back to me. They are very careful, and in the main I get them all back ; but instance after instance has occurred of their having unaccountably gone astray.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is not the point of the objection. The point of the objection was that it was lost anyway, however it was lost.
Suppose a dozen papers are lost, do you found on that fact an argument that thereafter neither the government nor a minister shall bring down original papers ?

The file from which quotations were made is in the custody of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries ; it being in his custody, he is entitled to take care of it. The House has power to order that that file be produced, and if the House so orders, it comes down in obedience to that order, becomes a matter of record, and goes into the charge of Mr. Clark, who becomes responsible for it. Going into his possession in that formal, constitutional way, it would require an order of the House to release it. Has that file come into the possession of the member who has it now or of the hon. member for Peel in that constitutional way ? They will not say that it has. It came into their possession for this reason, that the Minister of Marine had quoted from one or two documents in it. If I understand it, the hon. member for Peel or the hon. member for North Toronto might demand, and would be entitled under the rules of the House, that the Minister of Marine should take from that file the documents which he had quoted from and lay them on the table.
These are not documents upon documents; they are pages of one document.

Precisely ; but the hon. gentleman will not say that because one letter has been used as an argument, in a file containing the papers of years, and because as a matter of courtesy, at the personal request of a member, the minister allows him to have the whole of the file to look at, there is any power that would compel him to do it? The fact that he handed that file as a matter of courtesy to a member did not impose upon the clerk of the House the necessity of guarding it, as would have been the ease had it been brought down in response to a formal order of the House.

The clerk of the House understood it as such, because I was only able to obtain the document from him on the understanding that I would return it so that he might lock it up after the House adjourned.

I can understand that the clerk, finding a valuable file on the table, would be anxious that it should be
taken care of. But the hon. member for Peel claims that the clerk was permitted to give that file back to the minister who laid it on the table only on a formal order of the House to do so. If that is so, it seems to me that it could only come into the constitutional possession of the clerk as the result of a formal motion to lay it on the table. Surely if the action of the House is requisite in the one case it is in the other. If the minister in an informal manner lays a document on the table, can he not in the same informal manner withdraw it?
247 i
After quoting part of the papers ?

Yes. I grant that he would be required to leave on the table the papers which he quoted from out of that file. That would not be a matter of courtesy, but a matter of right; but he would not be bound to lay the whole file on the table.
But he did lay it on the table.
He laid it on the table in an informal way, retaining his right of control over it. Is the Minister of Marine not at liberty to take that file away to-night ?

Does the hon. gentleman want my answer ? If I ask the minister,
not as a matter of courtesy to me, but as a matter of right, after he has exercised his own right of quoting from that document and basing his argument upon it, to lay it on the table of the House, I have a perfect right to take the document and keep it for Hie reasonable time that is necessary for me to look up that which he quoted and everything cognate to it within the file.

I do not suppose that Mr. Speaker is to be asked for his decision on that point ; but I would be pleased to know whether that is the rule or not. I admit that papers quoted from must go into the possession of the House as a matter of course ; but the whole file, which was laid on the table in an informal way, and at the request of a member, must not go into the posession of the House unless with the consent of the hon. gentleman who places it before the House, and does so with the understanding that it is to be looked at, but is not to leave his possession. He certainly has a right to take it back, if he sees fit to do so.
Is there any rule for more?
I think so.
Read it.

I was going to submit this. If the point made by the Minister of Customs be correct, suppose an order had been given and then cancelled, and afterwards renewed, the House would be then misled into the supposition that that order had never been given. In this instance, one portion of a state document said the order had been cancelled; but afterwards, as the

lion, member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has pointed out, that same order had been given to another individual, of the same interested parties. By not producing the whole file, the House would then be misled into the belief that the order had never been given. You see therefore, if you give only one letter and not all the documents, how inconvenient that would be and how the House might be deceived. Does the hon. minister not think that in pursuance of our undoubted practice-and that I regard as authority- when a minister quotes a document that document has to be laid on the table, and it has to be laid there for a purpose. What purpose ? It is not that every member shall have an opportunity of informing himself with regard to it, and does that not imply that a reasonable time must be allowed members to examine that paper ? Can that opportunity be given when the paper is laid on the table a few minutes and before the discussion is through it is taken away, or before those who desire to see it have an opportunity of doing so. Does not the rule ] imply that there shall be u reasonable time given to allow the whole House to examine the document ?
I think not.
If not, then I do not know what rights this parliament has.

I am not questioning the right of parliament to ask for public documents and to get them. If the hon member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) was not satisfied, if he thought there were more papers on that file which he would like to see, he would move for them. I am simply speaking on the point of putting the documents in the possession of the House in the proper way.

The rule and the practice, as I take it, is that when public papers which are quoted by a minister of the Crown, are required to be produced for the information of the House-not the information of any individual member-in order to come to a correct conclusion upon the question, they must be laid on the table so that all can examine them.
Precisely.
And not one portion of the papers but the whole of them.

The document quoted from, which the minister has in his possession, has to be laid on the table, so that all the other members may have the same knowledge of it that the minister has. Might I ask the hon. member for North Toronto, (Mr. Foster) now? There were one or two letters quoted from a file the other day by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Suppose, instead of having the file before him, he had simply the two letters, Mr. SPROULE.
could you require the whole file to be laid on the table or just the two letters?

The minister might read the two letters, but if any hon. member came to the conclusion that it would be well to know whether those were the only two letters with reference to the subject, he could put the question. And if the minister replied that there were other letters, any hon. member would have the right to insist on his bringing down the whole correspondence.
Would the minister have to lay the whole file on the table without a motion being made ordering it to be produced?
He could not lay anything on the table that he did not have in his immediate possession.
But would an individual member have a right, on his mere request, to have the original file laid on the table?
Under those circumstances ?

Under any circumstances. If the minster had brought to the House simply the two letters from which he quoted, is there any rule which would compel him to lay on the table, not only those two letters, but any others? The letters he quoted, any hon. member might insist on his laying them on the table. But suppose the file were not here and a member would say there must be other letters which the minister has not read, would he not require to make a motion in order to have the file produced?
What I would do first would 1ft; to ask the minister to bring them down.
Would he be bound to bring them down?

Not unless he had an order of the House. But if he only read two letters out of the whole correspondence, any member could ask him to be kind enough to bring down the rest, and in nine cases out of ten the minister would consent. Of course he might refuse, and in that case I would make a motion.

The minister might do as an act of courtesy, just what the Minister of Marine and Fisheries did. The file was in his possession and could be taken away by him, with the exception of the documents he quoted from which must be laid on the table.

The Minister of Customs has probably been as long here as any hon. member in this House. Under ordinary circumstances, I would be inclined to accept his opinion, but I am afraid I can-

not do so in this instance. He does not seem to realize that once documents have been laid on the table of this House, they are in the possession of the House. Let me read -what I understand is an authority on the matter we are discussing :
It has been laid down by the highest authority that when a minister of the Crown quotes a public document in the House and founds upon it an argument or .assertion, that document, if called for, ought to be produced.
Yes.
What is the document?
The document that is quoted.
Suppose the Minister of Marine and Fisheries read half a letter, would he only be obliged to produce that half?
He would be obliged to produce that half certainly.
Nothing more, according to my hon. friend the Minister of Customs.
He would put the whole document from which he quoted.

If my hon. friend is right, he would have the right to cut that document in two and just place one-half on the table. He must be consistent. Surely the meaning of the rule is that, in a case of this kind, the whole file must be produced from which the minister quoted, just as he would have to produce the whole of a letter, and not merely the portion he read.

Even if the file should refer to a subject absolutely different from the one under discussion? The other night a document was quoted relating to the purchase of some fire extinguishers from Mr. Perreault. Because that document was quoted, was the minister obliged to bring down the whole file containing the dealings of the department with reference to fire extinguishers?
Is there any other correspondence on the file except that relating to the purchase and sale of fire extinguishers?
It is a file concerning fire extinguishers but the point brought up by the hon. member for Leeds was whether a certain letter had been signed by me or not. and that letter had to be produced.

I think we have drifted entirely away from the question as to who signed the letter before the controversy came up about placing on the table the file in question. From my experience in this parliament, I would have no hesitation in saying that the ordinary rule is that when a file of papers is quoted from, even if only one letter in it be quoted, the whole
file must be produced in order that the House may be able to judge whether there are any other letters to throw light on the subject. What is the object of placing a document on the table after it has been read? After an hon. member has heard a document read he knows all about that particular document. But he asks that the file be laid on the table in order that he may ascertain whether there is anything else in it bearing upon the question or not. That, to my mind, is what occurred in this instance.
But if the file was not in the House at all?

But the hon. gentleman quoted from the file, and I maintain that the file itself is the ' document ' referred to in the rule of Dr. Bourinot. Certainly,
I cannot put any other construction upon it. I look upon it, as the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has said, the same as if it were a bound volume. Suppose that these letters had been printed and bound in a book, and suppose the hon. gentleman had read from that book, would not he be obliged to lay the whole book on the table? And what is the difference, whether it is printed in a book and bound, or fastened together in the ordinary way of a file of letters in one of the departments? The minister asks: How if there are other subjects referred to in that file? But I understand that the practice in every department is to have a file for each subject. Certainly, that is what must be done if the business of the department is to be properly looked after; and that, I assume, is the case here. I understand that these letters refer to the one matter which we have been speaking about, and, if so, I can see no good reason for disconnecting one from the other. What right would even the minister have to open that file and take out a letter? I question very much the propriety of it. To my mind, a file is sacred, and, if this government went out of power today that file should be left in its entirety, no single document being taken from it Therefore, it would be impossible for the minister to lay one letter on the table without laying the whole on the table. If we apply reason and common sense to this question, we shall come to a better conclusion than by treating it in a technical way-and the treatment suggested is very technical to my mind. I express my opinion candidly, and I am perfectly serious in this matter. I think that the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) was quite entitled to have possession of the file on Saturday morning, or at such time as he desired. -I think the Minister of Marine and Fisheries made a mistake in going to the clerk, and asking, or demanding that the file should be handed over to him.

I am sure the hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) wishes to he fair

to me. Therefore, will he permit me a word at this point? The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) had that file for the whole evening, and was asked if he would be through with it that evening, and he said he would.
No.
I sent some one to him, and I certainly understood that he had said so.
No.
Will the hon. gentleman state what>he did say?

The hon. minister must not put words in my mouth. I asked the clerk for the file and it was given me with the understanding that I should return it to him before the close of the sitting, he saying that he must have it to lock it up in his safe.
Will the hon. gentleman deny that he told me, in the ' Hansard ' reporters' room, that he would probably need the file after eight o'clock, and would give it back to me. Does he deny that?
I am not here either to state or deny
Does the hon. gentleman deny it?
I do deny it emphatically; I never made such a statement. I never had such a thought in my mind, and the minister knows that very well.

Let us make this clear: The hon. gentleman denies formally that, after six o'clock, in the ' Hansard ' reporters' room, after I showed him the letters on the file, he said he would require it after eight o'clock, but he would give it to me after he was through.
That is an entirely different story. I told the clerk
No, I am speaking of what happened in the ' Hansard ' reporters' room

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is impossible to allow the discussion to go on in this way. An hon. member has the floor and unless he gives way
I am perfectly willing to give way, Mr. Speaker; but I do not wish to be deprived of my right.

What I say is this: The minister laid the file upon the table at my request. When I applied to the clerk for the file, the clerk said I could have it with the distinct understanding that I was to return it to him so that he could lock it up in his safe, as it was in his custody-that was the understanding he had. I took the file and went over it for an hour or two and returned it with the expectation that I Mr. BRODEUR.
should have an opportunity to get it again on Monday morning. But when I applied to the clerk for it, he told me that the minister had taken it away. He kept it all the rest of Friday, Saturday and Sunday and had not returned it up to three o'clock to-day. I said to the clerk that I would expect him to get it back from the minister, as it was in the custody of the House, and he said he would communicate with the hon. gentleman. He tried to get the minister by telephone, but was unable to do so. He then wrote a letter, asking the minister to return the file, but the minister had not returned it up to three o'clock. I asked the clerk if the file had been placed on the table at three o'clock, and he told me it had not. A few minutes after, the minister sent for me to go to his room. He said, ' Here is the file; what do you want from it?' I said that I did not know exactly, but I wanted him to return it to the clerk
Is that all the hon. gentleman said?

I said to the minister then that if he would bring the original file back to the clerk, I would not mention it in the House. That was my position. I wished to deal fairly with the minister, which I have done. But I may say the minister has not dealt fairly with me, and I will take another opportunity to refer to the matter.

I have very little more to add on this question. If any further evidence is required to show that the rule applies to the whole file and not to one particular letter that may happen to have been read, it is the fact brought out by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr.'Foster) that letter after letter, a continuation of letters, relating to this same matter is contained in the file. Surely, we cannot dissociate these other letters from the one read by the minister. They all go to constitute one document, and in no way can I understand the rule iald down by Bourmot unless it be applied as I have indicated.

I would ask the indulgence of the House for a moment, to correct in the same ' Hansard ' that it will appear in what appears to have been a mis-statement or not a full statement by the minister concerning these fire extinguishers bought in 1891. He stated that the old government, in 1891, bought two Babcock extinguishers at $30 each. He made other comments, that I will not allude to. What he did not state was this, that before these were bought, communication was had, both with Great Britain and the United States, and there is on file here a statement from F. A. Mahan, captain of engineers of the United States artillery, saying that they had called for competition and got the prices of some Babcock machines, and that as a result of

the competition they had taken six machines at $31.40 each. The price paid by the Marine Department here for these, after that report of the engineer, was $25 each.

Before you leave the chair I would like to say a few words with reference to an advertisement that has appeared lately with regard to a sale of the timber on a certain reserve on the French river known as the Dokis Indian reserve in the province of Ontario. I will read the first part of it :
There will be offered for sale by public auction, at an upset price, in the Russell House, in the city of Ottawa, on Wednesday, the 21th day of June, 1908, at the hour of ten o'clock in the forenoon, timber berths numbered 1 to 8 inclusive, covering the pine timber of nine inches diameter and over at the stump, and no other, on the whole of the Dokis Indian reserve, situate on the French river in the province of Ontario.
Each limit will be offered separately at a bonus, ten per cent of which to be paid in cash on day of sale, and notes to be given for the remainder, payable in three, six and nine months, at the Bank of Montreal, in the city of Ottawa, with interest at six per cent.
And there are other conditions of sale. With regard to this matter I asked a question, which was answered in the House last Thursday, on page 7735 of the ' Hansard.' In this answer it is stated that the notice regarding this sale was sent out from the department to certain newspapers, beginning in the 9th of April," and the list of newspapers is given. I may say that although the notice was said to be inserted iu the newspapers at that date, I received a notice from the deparment only on the 23rd of April. The list of newspapers is quite large ; of course they all appear to be Liberal newspapers. I do not know why this should be a matter of patronage to newspapers supporting the government, because it is a matter of business, and I fancy that every man in this House will agree that Conservatives are just as likely to buy these limits as Liberals. I think it would have been wiser for the government to advertise this sale in some Conservative newspapers, because some Conservatives do not take Liberal newspapers. I notice by this advertisement that the government propose to put an upset price on these limits. I desire to say that I think a reserve bid is much more effective in the selling of such a property than an upset price. Naturally many bidders, when they reach the upset price which has been made known before the sale, will not go any further ; whereas with a reserve bid, which is not made known to the bidders, there have been many instances in which limits have been sold for a great deal more money than the reserve bid. A reserve bid tends to bring a higher price from the bidders, because the limit purchasers naturally will be affected when they reach the upset price. With regard to the terms of payment, I find they have been made very easy in that only ten per cent of the bonus is to be paid in cash. This is a most unusual provision, because it is customary that from one-quarter to one-third of the bonus shall be paid in cash at the time of the sale, or within a few days afterwards. With regard to the notice of the sale of these limits, I may say frankly that at the proper season of the year the time allowed between the notice of sale and the auction would be sufficient, provided the lines between the different berths had been already surveyed. In the province of Ontario more notice is given than two months and a half. It is better to make the notice too long than too short. But this particular notice has been given at a most unfortunate time of the year. Frome the 9th of April when this notice was sent out, up to the present moment, it has been practically impossible for any person to go and examine that country. We all know that when spring comes on no one can get about in these woods, because there is still a good deal of snow on the land and ice on many of the lakes, and a person cannot go about either on snowslioes or by canoe. Therefore this notice is of no avail whatever up to the present time. The latter part of the month of May is usually a good time to travel in the country, but the Prime Minister will realize another objection when I say that there is no season of the year when there is as much danger of fire from prospectors as in the month of May. As soon as the snow is gone and the leaves get dry, there is more danger of fire than at any other season. For that reason also an unfortunate time has been selected for the sale of these limits. Then when the month of June comes on the flies get bad, and it is almost impossible for anybody to make a proper survey of the limit on account of the flies. Why the government should have chosen this particular time to give this notice I cannot understand, because it is the most unfortunate period in the whole year.
Now, the picking out of this time seems most peculiar for many reasons. I notice that the surrender by the Indians of their rights'to this timber and the authorization of the notice of sale were dated January 7, 1908. The Minister of the Interior recommended to council on February 20, 1908, that this surrender should be accepted and that the limits should be sold. The copies which I have do not show whether the order in council passed at that time for that purpose. But, if the sale could have been advertised in February then the number of weeks' notice given would have been amply sufficient. This timber is most valuable. It has been talked about by all the lumbermen

in this part of the country, to my certain knowledge for twenty five years. The old chief of these Indians who died, I think last year, always refused absolutely to agree to the sale of this timber, but, at certain times, the rumor would get about, that this timber was going to be sold. Therefore, it is not a new thing, it is something which has been in the eye of the lumbermen, at any rate, if not in the public eye, for twenty-five years at least. The Indians, having at last signed the surrender of their rights and having permitted the sale of this property, I submit that it is most extraordinary that after all these years of discussion, such a short notice should be given of the sale of this valuable property which, I am informed. will bring many hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Mr, FOSTER. If they get the proper price.

If they give a proper chance to the people to examine it and bid upon it. On Thursday last I put a series of questions to the government and I desire particularly to call attention to No. 4 :
Have the lines been run on the ground dividing the said reserve into the different timber berths which are advertised to be sold separately?
There are eight different berths within this Dokis reserve. I think there are about fifty miles of country altogether and it is proposed by the government to divide it up into eight berths. The answer which I received is as follows :
No, but a surveyor has been instructed to do the_work, and it is expected that he will be on the ground this week.
That is the part of this proposed sale to which I most strongly object and for which I think there is no justification whatever. The department sends out a blue print of this reserve showing it divided into eight berths which they propose to sell separately, but these lines have not been surveyed on the ground and any one knows that it is impossible for any cruiser or bush ranger to go there and make a proper estimate of each one of these berths unless there is a line for him to go by so that he may know what he is doing. In a property of this kind which is worth such a lot of money, a very small variation in these lines would* make a very great difference in the value of berths as compared with what it might be before and after the lines were actually run. With reference to the manner in which the advertisement was sent out, this was what was sent out to me from the department-a little clipping from a newspaper and a blueprint. Nothing is said to show that these lines have not been run. I do not happen to be personally interested in this matter. I have no intention of bidding on or buying in this property, but a person who received this Mr. PERLEY.
notice from the department would naturally take it for granted that these lines were run, he would send his men to examine that timber and if he did so they could not make a report on which he could bid for these different berths when they came up for sale.

Does not that blue-print state that it is a proposed sketch of the
survey ?

It says ' sketch showing timber berths in the Dokis Indian reserve, French river, Ontario, scale 3 miles to the inch.' At the bottom it says ' approximate areas.' It says nothing as to whether the lines are run or not.
That would show that they are not surveyed.

The hon. member for Nipissing knows full well that no one selling a limit guarantees the areas. Here it says ' Approximate areas.' If the ordinary expression had been used, it would say
*	more or less.'

Yes, but that is not the
approximate area.

I submit that the words
*	approximate area ' and ' so many miles, more or less ' mean the same thing. Under these conditions a man who did not know' that these lines had not been run would send his men up there to examine this country and they would be unable to present such a report as would enable him to bid on these different berths. The government, in this matter, are trustees for the Indians ; they should give every opportunity for the proper examination of this country in order that it may bring all that it is worth and I submit that no person selling this property for himself would give a notice at this time of year and without having the lines run. The government themselves cannot put an upset price on these limits without having the lines run, but perhaps they can do that later on themselves if'they get anybody who will undertake to do the work in the month of June and I presume that they cannot have it done before that.
In regard to the circumstances connected with the surrender of this reserve, which certainly, from the papers, seem to have been very peculiar, I do not propose to speak this evening, but probably they will be brought up later on in the session. I simply rose at this time, before it is too late, to call the attention of the government to this matter. I regret very much that the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) is not here this evening. I gave him notice today that I was going to speak on this but I have been unable to get a chance until this late hour. I want to urge upon the government-

My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) waited

until nearly eleven o'clock when, thinking that it would not come up, he went home.

I quite understand, it is unfortunate, but I want to urge upon the Minister of the Interior and the government, before it Is too late, to extend the time for this auction sale in order to give people who wish to bid a proper and reasonable chance to go and examine that country after the lines have been run on the field dividing these valuable berths one from the other. I thought that if it were brought to the attention of the government now they might act in the matter and as this property has been talked about and known for so many years, why should not the government be willing to wait a reasonable time before putting it up for auction sale and thus give every person, who might think that he would like to bid on these limits, a chance to know their full value in order that they may living all that they are worth. In that conection I would like to ask that the copies of the balance of the file to this date be brought down. This is reference No. 233 and the papers were asked for by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). As the Minister of the Interior is not here I would like to ask that copies of the balance of the papers in connection with this matter may be brought down promptly in order that we may have a chance to discuss the question a little more fully at some other time.

I am rather surprised to hear the hon. member for Argenteull, than whom there is probably no more practical lumberman in this country, take exception to the method of advertising this limit. I may say in the first place that the surrender was obtained from the Indians on the distinct understanding that they would not have to bear the fire risk during next season. That was the reason why a longer time was not given for the sale. However, there cannot possibly be any injury done to anybody, neither to the Indians nor to prospective buyers by reason of the length of time that will be available for exploring after the lines are run, because there are only altogether about 12 miles of line to run to divide the berths. Even from the blue print, anyone looking at No. 1 and No. 2 berths will see there is almost a natural line as there are two bays there one almost directly opposite the other. I think the line is only about a quarter of a mile across and it would only make a difference of a few trees anyway. I have been informed that a number of lumbermen are already on the ground. This reserve is well known and its value as a timber limit is well known also. The lumbermen have been trying to get a surrender from the late chief for years, but he always objected. There is not much wonder that he did object because he could look back at a time
when an almost equally valuable timber limit was sold by our friends on the other side of the House for the sum of three hundred and some odd dollars, to prominent politicians in this city. The chief naturally feared that something similar would happen had he consented to surrender the timber on this reserve. The lines will be completed and there will still be six weeks time to travel that country. It is not 100 miles out from civilization ; a man can leave here on the midnight train and be on the reserve the next evening. The Indians were given a positive pledge by the Indian agent who got the surrender, that they would not have to bear the fire risk this season.
There is nothing in the agreement with the Indians to that effect.

There was an understanding which is 1ust as binding as an agreement. There was a pledge given and were it not that the Indians have confidence in the agent that surrender could not have been obtained. There have been deputations of lumbermen as well as officers sent by the department, both by this government and previous governments, to that reserve to try and get a surrender not only in the interests of the lumber trade but in the interests of the Indians themselves because of the danger of that country being swept by fire, but hitherto the Indians refused to sell. There is no question at all about it but that that country will bring a very large amount of money. I would not like to risk an opinion because I have not examined the timber and know nothing about it except from hearsay, but the general expectation is that it will realize something in the neighbourhood of $1,000,000. I believe that when the sale comes on the day mentioned, it will be found that no mistake has been made as to the time and the competition will prove whether people have had time to explore it or not. There is only about 43 miles in it altogether and about one-third of the whole territory in which the line is almost marked out now. This is an island and it narrows down by two bays opposite each other to about a quarter of a mile in width, so that there Is no trouble in any bushman travelling that part of it even without a line. A man could not make a mistake of $500 worth in the difference between where the line will be and where he would plant it himself by looking at a blue print sketch.
What about the other six berths.

It means 10 or 12 miles of a line at the outside which would mean 10 or 12 days of a surveyor. The surveyor, who has been ordered to go there is well accustomed to that kind of work ; he has been doing it all his lifetime and is a very capable man. He certainly will run all

these lines in 12 days, so that there will be six weeks time to travel 43 miles.
Oh. no.

Oh, yes, and even if there was only one month it is ample time. Having regard to the pledge given the Indians there was no possibility of extending the time and keeping faith with them. I happen to know about that, because I was instrumental in getting the agent appointed as I had every confidence in him and one of the reasons why I wanted him appointed was in order to get the surrender of this and another reserve. I felt that it would be for the benefit of the Indians as well as for the benefit of the whole country, because the timber surrounding has been cut and the limit was in very great danger from fire and of course if it was burned it would be no good to the Indians or any one else. As to the terms, they are exactly the terms given by the Ontario government in all their large sales. That is, with the exception that the present Ontario government have lately been selling by the thousand feet instead of by the mile, and they take the risk of fire. The purchaser may leave that timber standing until a year before the term of the lease expires, and then he can go in and cut and in the meantime they put up a small deposit and the government takes all risk. There was the sale of a township at the head of Garden river a short time ago where $10.52 per 1,000 feet board measure was obtained for the limit and $2 dues making $12.52, and it was held up as being a tremendous sale. But you must take into consideration that the government carried the fire risk for 15 years, or rather for 14 years because the timber could be cut in the last year. In the present instance the intention is that the Indians will not have to take the fire risk but that the purchaser of the timber will. With regard to an upset price or a reserve bid, I do not know that there is very much difference between the two. I do not know that the up-set price means that the price is to be made public. I doubt very much if it is. It does not necessarily have to be told to the auctioneer until the sale is in progress. I do not quite understand why the hon. member (Mr. Perley) said the upset price was to be made public for I am quite sure such is not the intention of the Minister of Indian Affairs. If I understand it aright an upset price means the same thing as a reserve bid. You can rest satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that there is no such thing as the upset price being made public at all ; the upset price is to be made known to the auctioneer at the time of the sale aud not before.
If the hon. gentleman bought the right from the Indians on the 7th of January, and would probably sell, would he have had those lines run before I
this time, or would he have waited to have them run within a month of the sale ?

Does the hon. gentleman sate that the government were in a position to advertise it in January ? My information is that they were not. My information is that there was not one minute lost from the time of the surrender until it was advertised. There were some conditions put in the surrender which were not satisfactory, and these were only arranged later. That is my information. I am quite sure that the government were not in a position to advertise the sale in January.

Mr. Speaker, before we go into Supply, I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Railways and Canals to a very serious matter. I have been notified this evening by telephone that a dam belonging to the government at Valleyfield has broken and the waters of Lake St. Francis are overflowing to such an extent that barns, stables and even dwellings are threatened to be carried away, and the people are fleeing from the place. I would ask the hon. Minister to send an engineer to-morrow morning to see what can be done. Lake St. Francis is a part of the St. Lawrence river.

Mr. Speaker, in this connection I would like to bring up the matter that I spoke of the other day, namely, the breaking away of a portion of the same embankment at Ste. Barbe in the county of Huntingdon. After the embankment broke this year I addressed a letter to the minister in regard to the matter. The land there is splendid farming land, and the people bought it and cultivated it believing that the government would protect the embankment. This break occurred at a time when the farmers were ready to put in their grain. I would urge the minister to get a report from his engineer in regard to making the embankment secure so that the people will not be drowned out every year.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways aud Canals).
speechtext:
The question raised by the hon. member for Beauharnois (Mr. Bergeron) is a very serious one. The difficulty this year is that the water in the St. Lawrence is higher by several feet than it has been in the memory of the oldest residents along the river. We have been notified that thousands of dollars of damage has been done in the Thousand Islands owing to the water having risen above high-water mark. I will act on the suggestion of my hon. friend and send a man down to-morrow morning to see what can be done. With regard to the matter mentioned by the hon. member for Huntingdon,

it is difficult to say what can be done in this exceptional year ; but in an ordinary year protection ought to be afforded.

I would like to ask the Prime Minister if after hearing the somewhat lengthy discussion on the fire extinguisher matter to-night, he will consult his Minister of Marine, and have all the original documents laid on the table, so that the members may examine them at a later day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I thought that after all that had been said on the subject it had been exhausted, and that there was nothing more to be said.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we go into Supply, I beg to call attention to a dispatch which I find to-day in the Toronto ' World ' and which is also published in the Toronto ' Mail.' It purports to come from Montreal and reads as follows :
Will the government come down to parliament and admit that a mistake has been made in the location of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway hundreds of miles north of the big cities, instead of starting from North Bay or thereabouts, thus easily tapping Montreal and Toronto ?
This is a question a good many wise men are asking here to-day. One thing is certain, there is a big ' something ' in the wind.
The Grand Trunk noon train to-day brought down Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Hon. Sydney Fisher and Hon. ltodolphe Lemieux, and it was soon evident that the mission was an important one.
Of course the matter of an interview with Premier Gouin was readily admitted, and as a matter of fact this interview took place, but the meeting between Mr. Hays and the Prime Minister was of another kind.
Those who are familiar with the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific officials declare that a grievous apprehension of coming difficulties has settled down upon both for some reason or other, and the statement is made that the trouble is all over what is said to have been the awful blunder made in the location of the transcontinental away from the freight and passenger producing centres of the country.
It has now- become painfully evident to the ministers and company alike-so the story goes-that Fitzpatrick and Parent must have intentionally or no, pulled the wool over their colleagues' eyes, and to-day the latter are committed to what one man styled ' the most stupendous blunder ever perpetrated in this or any other country.'
A prominent railway man said to-day that he had never vet understood why Toronto and Montreal looked on with so much apathy and indifference while the matter was before parliament.
' But,' he said (and his name if divulged would carry tremendous weight, both in parliament and the country), ' even at this late hour Sir Wilfrid should face the situation, admit the error and put the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific right before the country and posterity.'
It is a well-known fact here that all concerned are greatly worried, and it only remains to be seen if the proper parties will have the courage to grapple with the question of the modified route in the way that it should be grappled with.
I have to say that whoever penned that paragraph for the press had not even a shadow of reason for so writing. That there has been any hesitation or doubt as to the proper location of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway has never come to my knowledge or even been hinted to me or expressed in any way. When it is said that ' all concerned are greatly worried,' I have to say that we are not worried at all, and that the matter referred to has not engaged the attention of any one so far as I know. The statement that I went to Montreal for the purpose of interviewing somebody in respect to this matter is also another fallacy. I do not know for what purpose this statement is published-evidently to create suspicion in the minds of somebody and to arouse Toronto and Montreal, which are not on the line of the railway. If that is not the object of the dispatch, I know not what the ob'ect is. But I have to repeat that there is not a shadow of foundation for the statements made.
My right hon. friend has no doubt overlooked the question that I put to him in respect to the original documents.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, I have not overlooked it. I thought my hon. friend had exhausted all he had to say on the matter and that the House had also.
I asked the right hon. gentleman if after hearing this long discussion he would instruct the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to lay the original documents on the table of the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand, Mr. Speaker, that in accordance with your ruling the minister has laid the papers on the table of the House for the reasonable inspection of members, the same to be returned to him afterwards.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Public buildings, Ontario-North Bay public buildings, $17,500.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext:
Petitions were received for the erection of this building from the municipal association, the board of trade, the ' mayor and some two hundred people. Up-

wards of a dozen properties were submitted to the government's agent, Mr. P. McCool. After examination, he secured options on eight. The department then sent an expert, Mr. Hewitt, to make an examination, ami he selected four with the purpose of getting offers. The site finally approved of cost 92 cents per square foot. The next most eligible site was offered at $2.31 per foot. The other sites were low lying, required expensive draining and were not central. The agent reported the price of 62 cents per foot as fair and reasonable. My hon. friend from Nipissing (Mr. McCool) will corroborate my statement when I say that the property acquired by the department for $8,100 was valued by many people at as much as $10,000 and could have been sold afterwards for that sum. It was bought from Mr. William Doran. The site is 66 feet on Queen street and 132 feet on Fraser street.
Any buildings ?
Some old buildings.
It is a large price ?
North Bay is growing rapidly. The next eligible lot was offered at $11,000 or $2.31 per foot.
What is the population?
At present between 5,000 and 6,000.
Is this for post office and custom house?
Yes, and an armoury as well. All in one building.
What will be the total cost?
$61,373 including site, heating, electric wiring, fittings, &c.
Who has the contract ?
McGillivray and P. Lebel of Ottawa. The contract price is $33,879.
Were there many tenders?
Nine, and the lowest was accepted.
How much has been done?
On the 15th December, $33,511.03.
Who is the inspector?
The clerk of works is Mr. William Martin.
He is a builder and a practical man.
That is a departure from the ordinary rule.

When it was decided to erect a public building there I was asked Mr. PUGSLEY.
with regard to the site. I went to North Bay and placed the selection in the hands of the mayor at that time, who is now custom house officer, Mr. William Mackenzie, and the president of the board of trade. The president of the board is a very prominent Conservative politician as well as one of the leading citizens of the place. I asked them to select a number of sites and mark them Nos. 1, 2 and 3 and so on, in order of preference, and I handed them over to a namesake and a cousin of mine in the real estate business. And if any one should inquire as to his fitness for that kind of work, he will find that it was given into proper hands. They handed a list of the sites to Mr. McCool who got options on them and sent them down to the department. The minister sent up a representative and he made a selection. I had nothing whatever to do with it and had no preference for one property over another. The site chosen is considered the most suitable. Mrs. Doran was offered $10,000 for the property for commercial purposes, but she had sufficient interest in the town to give her preference to the department. Her interest was perhaps not altogether unselfish because her son was running one of the large hotels at the time and this site was within reasonable distance of it. and no doubt it would add to the value of his business to have this public building in its immediate vicinity. Otherwise she would not have been justified in taking $1,500 less than other people offered her. $8,500 was the original price but there was a building on it which sold for $400. making the net price $8,100. At that price, the property was the best bargain in North Bay for years. The town is very prosperous. It has a population of not less than 6.000 people at present. When the census was taken, its population was only 2.500, but the country north has increased since the census from 1,300 to 40,000. When this question was up here Friday, I think some hon. member on the other side said that North Bay would not be much after the Toronto-Sud-bury line was running. But North Bay will still be North Bay even after that line is built, because there is a tremendous country for which it is the distributing point.
I understand the minister to say that the total contract for the building is $33,000. Does that include heating and lighting ?
No, that is for the building only.
With $33,000 for the building .and $8,000 for the site, how does the minister make up this $60,000 ?

The site cost $8.100; survey of site, legal expenses and clerk of works' salary. 1901-3. paid the contractor to 15th December. 1907. $22,510 ; total pay-

rnents, 832,511.03. Amount due on contract, $11,369 ; heating and boilers, $4,500 ; electric wiring and fixtures, $1,500 ; fittings, furniture and lock boxes, $6,000 ; sidewalks, and fencing, $500 ; contingencies and superintendence, $4,993-total, $61,373.03.
Is the contractor to receive more than this $33,000 ?
There appear to be no extras.
Is the electric light to be put up by contract ?
This is not a contract, but an estimate.
I may state, for the information of the committee-and I am very sory to say it-that the contractor has lost money. The excavation was of very hard rock.
We ought to get his picture.
The minister is increasing the wages of the clerk of works to $4 a day. In the discussion we had last week, I did not notice any case in which the pay was over $3 a day.
The further we go west the higher wages we have to pay to gentlemen in these positions. In British Columbia we have to pay considerable more.
You only pay $4 a day in British Columbia, do you not ?

No, more. I am advised by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Mc-Cool) that the services of a competent man for this work could not be had for less than $4 a day. In British Columbia we are paying $5.50 and even more.
Do you pay these men for Sundays ?
I presume so. But I intend to try to make an arrangement in future under which they will not be paid for Sundays. Of course, if you figure it on a monthly basis, it will come to the same thing.
No, figuring by the day they will not claim wages for Sundays.
This clerk of works has already received over $600. What does the minister expect the total pay of the clerk of works to be ?
I am told that the building is about completed, with the exception of the fittings.

You do not need the services of a clerk of works for the fittings, do
you ?
Mi-. PUGSLEY. I think we would require somebody to see to it that the work
is done according to the plans and specifications. At all events, we shall soon be able to dispense with his services.
Was he a contractor or builder V
A builder. .
Yes, and he took contracts occasionally.

I will ask to take up again some of these Kingston items. I would ask for a reconsideration of the item (or a new gun-shed, with a view to striking [DOT]it out. A new plan is under consideration by the Militia Department for the erection of a barracks. If that is carried out, tiie gun-shed would form part of the new building. I move the reconsideration and striking out of the following items :
Kingston-new gun shed, $10,000.
Motion agreed to.

Now, I move the reconsideration and striking out of the following item :
Kingston Artillery park-new guard house, including offices, &c., $8,000.
What is the object of striking it out?

This would come into the scheme of the new barracks, for which the Department of Militia is going to ask an appropriation, which appropriation, perhaps, will appear in the supplementary estimates of this year.
I take this opportunity of congratulating the minister on his economy. It appears that the result is to be a very much larger expense.
Motion agreed to.

I move the reconsideration and striking out of the following item:
Kingston-new hospital for ' A ' and ' B ' batteries, $10,000.

Now-, the following item was allowed to stand:
Kingston, Royal Military College-new servants' quarters, $10,000.
I have some information as to that. The information I have from the deputy minister is that these quarters are for the civil subordinates as well as for the riding school attachment. The building is for four non-commisioned officers and for 12 civil subordinates.
That doesn't explain anything.
These are for the married men's quarters.

It would be better to leave all the military buildings, because I have not got full information.

Leamington public building, $7,000.
How much is going to be spent at Leamington?
It is expected that the building will cost about $20,000. This estimate is to purchase land and make a commencement.
Leamington is a small place in the county of Essex. What peculiar claims has the town of Leamington for a post office?

To begin with, the census of 1901 shows a population of 2,451. Then the town of Leamington is second only to Windsor, in the county of Essex, in the extent of its population, and it stands next to Windsor and Walkerville in the amount of revenue derived from the post office, customs and inland revenue. These three services will be accommodated in the new building. In some years the inland revenue lias amounted to $14,000. It has a number of factories, and does a large trade in lumber. It is being supplied with natural gas.

I concede that Leamington is a thriving town, but I would like to know what rule is adopted by the department according to which post offices are supplied. It strikes me from the public buildings that I see being voted, that the chief qualification must be that the county shall be represented by a supporter of the government.

If the hon. gentleman had been here when we discussed this matter last, he would have heard that in Sherbrooke, London and Brantford, which places are represented by Conservatives, the government are putting up public buildings. I think the hon. gentleman will find evidence that we are endeavouring as far as possible to meet the requirements of the people in respect to public buildings, irrespective of political considerations. It is also just possible that our friends may be a little more insistent in asking for public buildings than our opponents.

I have been begging for a long time for a drill hall for the town of Dunnville in which I live. We have a fine militia company there, and we cannot get accommodation for them. We are also in great need of a post office. I think there is no town in the province of Ontario that is worse off than we are, when the size of the place is considered. I think it is a far more important town than Leamington. I notice in the next county the town of Welland, which has not only a new drill hall but also a fine post office and customs house.
What is the population of your town?
I think 2,800. We have no public building of any kind whatever,

either drill hall or post office. I think in the disbursement of public money for these purposes some consideration should be given to other counties than those sending Liberals to this House. I hope the Minister of Public Works will give my county a little more consideration than it has received in the past.
I shall certainly give the matter careful consideration.

The present minister is new to his office, but if he will look up the records of his department he will find that one of his predecessors sent out a circular asking members and defeated candidates to send in requests for public buildings.

I have enough requests without sending out circulars inviting more.
Ottawa departmental buildings-renewal of skylights, $6,000.

This is asked for by the chief architect for renewal of the present skylights in the new departmental buildings. It is for the purpose of providing metal skylights including flashings. There was an appropriation in 1907-8 which was not used. We are asking for a revote.
What departmental buildings are these-the eastern and western blocks ?
Yes.
Is that under contract ?
It is not yet.
' Is it going to be done by contract ?
I do not know.
I do not understand how the work can be done for that amount ?
If it cannot be done we will do as much as we can.
That seems a large price for simply putting in these metal windows.
They are skylights, and the work will be somewhat extensive.
The department know exactly how many skylights have to be renewed and there should be no difficulty in asking for tenders.
We have a carpentering and glazier's department in connection with the Public Works Department.

If it can be done by tender, I will certainly have it done in that way.
Ottawa Printing Bureau-electric motor machinery, $6,000.

This is a vote of $6,000 to provide for electric motors for the new machines that are being installed at the Printing Bureau The total probable cost is $20,504. There was a vote previously and we are asking now for $6,000. The assumed expenditure of $11,176 to the end of the fiscal year added to the $6,000 which we are now voting and $2,000 which was expended to December 31, 1907, makes a total of about $20,000.
Owen Sound public building, $50,000.
This is a vote which is asked to make provision for completing, during the present fiscal year, the public building which is under contraction at Owen Sound.
What is the total cost ?
The total probable cost including site is $90,000.
Owen Sound is not a large town ?
