Yes. This building is to be 82 by 52, with two storeys and basement.

Why do you provide
such a large building ?
This is to be used for the post office, customs and inland revenue.
We have the sarile in my town and the building there only cost $14,000.
Your town, of course, is very much smaller than Owen Sound.
What is the population ?
About 12.000.
In 1901 the population was 8,776. Owen Sound, I believe, is one of the best harbours if not the best natural harbour upon the Georgian bay. *
What rent have you been paying for the post office and customs house ?
The postal revenue is $16,865, customs duties, $45,000 ; excise, $40,000 ; money orders issued, $40,000 and money orders paid, $65,000.
What did the site cost ?
I cannot give my hon. friend from Kings and Albert the rental that was paid. The site cost $10,000.
Pretty high, is it not ?
It is a very finely situated lot with 70 feet frontage on Baker street and 95 on Scope street. My hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Telford) is not here.

He would be in favour of it.
Mr. FOWLER, Perhaps it may be the same with him as with the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Zimmerman) whose speech appeared in the Hamilton ' Herald ' or ' Times ' although that hon. gentleman was not here to deliver it.
I was not responsible for it.
I am not saying that the hon. gentleman was responsible, but it shows a strong imagination on the part of the reporter of the ' Times.'

I think the newspaper should be excused. I made the statement just as the hon. member for Hamilton was going out that the item would be passed and by mistake, they have reported the speech as having been delivered by Mr. Zimmerman instead of Mr. Henderson.

May I ask the minister what newspjapers the advertisement appeared, when tenders were asked for the Owen Sound building ? I notice that $353 was paid for advertising. Does not my hon. friend think that is a large amount ?
That would take in the Toronto daily papers and my deputy tells me that it was advertised in about thirty different papers.
Does my hon. friend think any of these would be Liberal-Conservative papers ?
I would hardly suppose so, unless I had information to that effect.
My hon. friend was, the other evening endeavouring to lay down the policy that there was no politics in advertising for tenders.

No, what I told my hon. friend was that if I anticipated that the circumstances should arise that the advertising could not be widely circulated by the insertion of the advertisement in Liberal papers, I would not hesitate to avail myself of Conservative papers.
I may say that I think the newspaper having the largest circulation in the town is the Liberal-Conservative paper.

Owen Sound is the county town of my county. It has a population of 12,000 and almost adjoining it is the village of Brook with a population of

7S20
about 2,000. The nearest large towns to Owen Sound are Durham, 28 miles to the south, Meaford, 18 to 20 miles east, and Wiarton, 25 miles northwest, so that Owen Sound does business with a very large territory. It has one of the finest harbours on the lakes and during last winter there was tied up in that harbour a larger amount of shipping than in perhaps any other harbour in Ontario ? The site chosen for the post office met with the approval of all the people of the town, and it is considered a very fine one. As to the circulation of the newspapers referred to by the hon. member for Peel, I do not know which of the three papers has the largest circulation but I should say it was between the Owen Sound ' Times ' the Conservative paper, and the Owen Sound ' Sun ' one of the Liberal papers. The Owen Sound ' Sun ' is published twice a week and the Owen Sound ' Times ' once a week.
Will the minister lay on the table a list of the papers in which this advertisement was published.

I will be glad to.
Mr. BLAIN1. The hon. member for East Kent (Mr. Gordon) stated the other night that the ' London Advertiser ' had about the same circulation as the London ' Free Press.' I have here a certified statement which gives the daily average circulation of the London ' Free Press ' as 19,589 and the daily average circulation of the ' Advertiser ' at 11,827. I again ask the minister if he will publish advertisement with reference to the Glencoe building in the London ' Free Press ' which has the largest circulation in that section of the province.

I cannot promise the hon. gentleman, but I should think that the ' Advertiser ' with a circulation of 12,000 (if that figure is correct) would afford sufficient publicity. It must be remembered that the advertisement is published in several Toronto papers one of which is the ' Globe ', and I think my hon. friend will admit that the Toronto ' Globe ' has a much larger circulation in Ontario than any Conservative newspaper; its circulation is twice or three times as large.
Not at all.
My hon. friend (Mr. Blain) would not suggest that there was any want of wide circulation for this advertisement seeing it was published In thirty different newspapers.
My point is that the minister is using this large amount of public money for political purposes.
Oh, no. ,

The minister will not say that any single one of these thirty news-Mr. MILLER.
papers was a Liberal-Conservative newspaper. If he will frankly admit that the policy of the department is to put these advertisements in Reform papers and refuse them to Liberal-Conservative papers I can understand him.

I told my hon. friend that I would only avail myself of the columns of Conservative papers in cases where I felt it was necessary to give wider circulation by doing so. I may say to my hon. friend that we make out a list of newspapers in Tillich advertisements for works in the district are to be inserted and every day we are refusing to give our friends advertisements. We feel that by advertising in newspapers in the district and surrounding cities where the works are to be carried out that we are giving ample publicity and we do not yield to the request of our friends to extend the patronage.
How will a Conservatitve contractor know about these works if he only takes a Conservative newspaper.
He would not be so narrow as that.
We have not found any difficulty in that direction. We find that Conservative contractors tender and they always get fair play.
Would it not be much cheaper and do just as well to advertise in the ' Canada Gazette.'
I do not think so.

It seems to me that you are spending too much money on advertising, and that if these advertisements were published only in the ' Canada Gazette ' they would reach contractors and builders all over the country because if such were known they would all take the ' Canada Gazette '. I do not find fault with the minister giving these advertisements to the Liberal newspapers.
You think I would be an anomalous sort of individual if I did otherwise.

If I were running a Liberal newspaper and you advertised in a Conservative organ and not in my paper I would feel dissatisfied. We do not run a political department the same as we run a Sunday school, and you are expected to give the patronage to your friends. That part of it is all right. But, if these advertisements were only published in the ' Canada Gazette' they would reach all the contractors who would be on the outlook for them. A contractor living in Ottawa might tender on a building in New Brunswick and as we know the Sussex building was erected by an Ottawa contractor. It might be a little tough on the newspapers to advertise only

In the ' Gazette ' but it would be satisfactory.
It would be a great departure from the practice of the last forty years and I fear it would be said that I was not giving sufficient publicity.

It would be said that you were not giving sufficient pap to the newspapers that are supporting you. The hon. gentleman need not be afraid of a new departure because he is supposed to be a Liberal now and Liberals are always making departures.

I have some sympathy with the suggestion made by the hon. member (Mr. Fowler). I have often thought it would be a good idea to have one standard publication in which these contracts would be advertised, and the contractors all over the country knowing of that would look out for these advertisements. With reference to the Owen Sound public building, I do not agree with the hon. member for South Grey that it is necessary to spend this large amount of money for a public building even in the thriving town of Owen Sound. It seems to me that for a great deal less, ample accommodation could be furnished for the Post Office, Customs and Inland Revenue Departments. To my mind, this would be an admirable case in which, if the government are determined to spend $90,000 in a county they could divide it up among the various towns in the county. I do not know that there is a public building in South Grey or in East Grey. We do not ask the government to increase the expenditure; I would be very sorry to do that: but by dividing the expenditure amongst the different towns and villages in a county, the minister could provide ample accommodation in the county town. and small public buildings in other towns and villages. I hope the minister will take this into consideration.
The minister seems to think that $90,000 is a very trifling sum for a custom house in the town of Owen Sound, with a population of 7,000 or 8.000 people.
Twelve thousand.

The hon. member for South Grey has made a census of his own, and says 12,000; but he does not know any more about the population of Owen Sound than I do. I would remind the minister that in the city of Fredericton the parliament house, a very handsome and commodious building, was erected and completed at a cost of only $108,000.
When was that built?

About twenty-five years ago. It is a large and handsome building of stone, a credit to the province, and it cost only $18,000 more than you are going 248
to spend on this custom house in the little town of Owen Sound.

I think the minister told us that the postal revenue of Leamington was $14,000 and that of Owen Sound, $16,000. A $7,000 public building is good enough for Leamington, but $90,000 is to be spent on one in Owen Sound.
The excise revenue in Owen Sound was $40,000.

I am speaking now of the postal revenue. I quite agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Halton. that there should be some arrangement by which some of the public money would be spent on the smaller towns and villages. I think they are entitled to some consideration. It does seem to me that $90,000 for a public building in Owen Sound is excessive, and that there are many other places that are equally entitled to be provided for.

Owen Sound is one of the towns I know something about. It is one of the principal gateways to eastern t anada from the Great Lakes and has perhaps the best natural harbour in the western part of this province. Along a stretch of fifteen miles, a disabled vessel can get in and be in perfect safety. Last year they did a large business. It has large elevators and handled some 6,000,000 bushels of grain and expects to handle more. I have a good deal of sympathy with the idea of the government spending money on good buildings wherever there are a revenue and population to justify it. I do not take the ground at all that we ought to be parsimonious although we ought not to be extravagant. This money is placed where necessity demands it and we should take into consideration the necessity for a building and not say promiscuously that we ought to spend so much in the country and so much in the town. That is not a business way of looking at it.

Why not ? Is not the country entitled to public buildings as
well as the town ?

I said where the business needs it. We ought not to say that we shall give so much to the country villages and so much to the towns without recard to the needs and interests of the different places. The Inland Revenue at Owen Sound is something like $40,000 last year. The postal revenue is about $16,000 and the customs about $45,000 or over $100,000 year-1 v revenue. In the smaller places, my hon. friend from Haldimand forgets that they iust require post offices whereas here we have three services in the one building. The Dominion ought to take pride in having a good building where there is a large revenue and also out of regard for the safety of the service we ought to have a fireproof building. Owen Sound is one of most



thriving places in the Dominion. It has the situation and the enterprise and to this day they have never had a government building there. For the present needs this building may be a little large, but it is wise economy to look to the future and I believe that no more justifiable expenditure could be made by any public department.

I think the hon. minister must be mistaken when he said the revenue of the post office at Leamington was $14,000 and at Owen Sound $16,000.
Mr. LALOR, From the latest report, the town of Dunville in my constituency has a postal revenue of $4,437 and it has no post office.
I did not give the postal revenue at Leamington as $14,000. I said that the Inland Revenue was that amount and the postal revenue $3,375.

Dunnville has a postal revenue of $4,437 and Leamington $3,177. The money order revenue at Dunnville is $15,759, Glencoe $9,773 and Leamington $12,750. Much smaller places get magnificent bulid-ings while Dunnville, which is much more important, cannot get them. The government should take into consideration the importance of the town and the public revenue collected there, and should not make it their first consideration that the town elects a supporter of the government. Towns of less importance should not be given public buildings while the more important ones are suffering,
. Mi\ BLAIN. I want to attract my hon. friend's attention to the large increase in expenditure over the Estimates first made when the votes are first asked for. For instance in 1906 the Estimates for the building at North Bay was given at $14,000 by the ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Hyman). Now my hon. friend says the total cost will be about $60,000.
Probably my predecessor did not include the site and fittings and furniture. The contract was for $33,000.

There may be something in that. The estimate for the Owen Sound public building, when the vote was first asked, was between $40,000 and $50,000. The ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Hyman) said it would depend on whether the building was to be of stone or brick. Now-' we have the minister saying that the cost will be $90,000, almost double. I hope my hon. friend will be more careful and see that his estimates are more in accord with the total expenditure. The opposition are alw'ays tw'itted with having consented to these expenditures, but after voting certain amounts, they are then asked to vote a great deal more than was estimated and when objection is raised they are asked if they are going to refuse money to complete Mr. GRAHAM
the work after so much has been expended on it. As the minister is new to the department and is reforming it on every hand, I hope he will see that his department in future will give a correct statement of what these buildings will cost. I am quite sure that this is one of the ways in which the enormous expenditure of which the people of Canada are complaining is arising and taking possession of the government-and, I fear, is mastering some of the departments.

I have been a good deal impressed by the arguments of some hon. gentlemen opposite-my hon. friend from Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler), my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) and others-as to the reasonable demands of the people for erecting buildings in the smaller towns throughout the country.	I entirely
sympathize with that view.	In towns
where there is no other very considerable expenditure of public money, even though the population of such towns may not be very large, it is not unreasonable that they should have the accommodation afforded by a public building. They contribute to the revenue of the country proportionately to people living in larger cities and towns. But we must be patient; we cannot erect all these buildings at once, as some of our friends would like us to do. If I am to judge by some of the expressions of our friends opposite, instead of providing for a moderate number of buildings, such as I have provided for, they would like a public building for every town in the country.
I have not suggested anything of that kind.
Well, I hope our friends will be patient.

When this matter was discussed a few days ago, I think I did not make myself clear. I stated the population of Leamington at 2,451. The population of Aylmer is about the same. Now, with regard to the town of Aylmer, I would like to call attention to the fact that the postal revenue of that town is $4,459; the amount of money orders issued about $20,000. I did not bring out these facts the other day when I was speaking about the matter.
Aylmer is a very nice town. I am going to try to go there. Will the hon. gentleman promise me, if I go, that he will not accuse me of trying to bribe the people?

I will undertake to take the minister out and show him a good country. Let me add to what I already said that we have one of the largest canning factories in Canada, also a large condensed milk factory, large iron works and other manufactories. Aylmer is a very important town As I understand it, the

reason given for not building a post office in Aylmer before now is that we have not made claims. I intend to keep on making claims, and I hope to be successful.
Port Arthur public building-addition, $10,000.

Of this, $2,000 is a revote. It is for the erection of a one-storey brick addition on a stone foundation, in rear of the existing building, extending from the examining warehouse towards Court street. The new building will be 38 by 36 feet.
What will be the total cost?

The contract is for $7,475. It is estimated that heating and lighting will cost $1,000, fittings and furniture, &c., $2,000; contingencies and superintendence, $1,548.	Tenders were called
for by public advertisement and two tenders were received, one for $7,475 and the other for $10,000. The lowest was accepted.
I have had some experience in building, and I must say this seems an awful price for a building 38 by 36 feet. It is only a plain building, I understand- a sort of warehouse.

It is an examining
warehouse. It is very substantially built- very large girders carried on iron columns.
Renfrew public building, $10,000.

This building is to be of stone on a concrete foundation. The main portion is to have a frontage of 50 feet, and 40 feet in depth, with two storeys, basement and attic; and addition in the rear 27 by 27 feet, and two storeys high.
What is to be me total cost?
Including everything, $41,154.06. This is for both post office and customs house.
Are there to be any extras?
There is a contract for $24,500, and I think there is no estimate of extras.
What is the population of Renfrew, and what is its revenue?

In 1901, the population was 3,153; postal revenue, $5,212.79; customs revenue, $3,392.89; money orders issued, $26,681.89; money orders paid, $27,681. Renfrew has a fine water-power. There are there a foundry, tannery and woollen, saw, flour and planing mills.
This building is altogether too expensive ; $20,000 would be enough.

I would be glad to cut these buildings to $20,000, but it is pretty difficult.
24Si

It is not difficult at all. Put your foot down and say that the building shall not cost more than a certain price, and tell your architect he must draw the plans accordingly. The public building in my town houses the post office and inland revenue, and is ample for the purpose, and it cost $14,000 equipped.

I am going to see what I can do.
St. Mary's public building, $12,000.
This is for a public building in the town of St. Mary's, in South [DOT]Perth. The total cost is estimated at $40,819.23.
An outrage again.
You can hardly call it an ' outrage,' though you might say we might erect a smaller and cheaper building That is possible. In future. I am going to try to cut the prices down.
What was the cost of the site ?
It was $2,300.
What is the population of St. Mary's ?
Quite a large town- 3,384.
The total post office revenue is $5,740, and we are expending $40,000 upon the post office in a town with a revenue of a little over $5,060.
But you must remember that this building is for post office, customs and inland revenue purposes. The customs revenue alone is over $13,000.

It strikes me that the expenditure is far in excess of the importance of a town of the size of St. Mary's. I urge again the same objection, that sq large an amount of' money is being expended in one town while another town is overlooked.

We are endeavouring j:o cut down the cost below the sum asked for,, and we are endeavouring to do the same with all these votes. The contract price of this builing is $22,500. The town is in the county of South Perth.
Why is it costing $40,000, when the contract price is only $22,500 ?

We have to take into account the cost of the site, heating, fittings, furniture, and lock boxes, which alone cost $5,000 Inspection is included in the survey of the site. Contingencies and sunerin-tendence, $3,009. Survey of site, legal and travelling expenses, printing and advertising. salaries and superintendence, amount to a little over $5,000. The plans were prepared in the department.
How long will this contract last ?

The contract was dated in September, 1906, and the building is to be completed by the 15th of December, 1907. There are the travelling expenses of the architect to and from Ottawa to examine the building from time to time. It may be that the $3,000 for contingencies will not be all used.
Who is the architect ?
1 have not the name of the architect.
Was the inspector appointed by the patronage committee of the town?
I do not know that there is any patronage committee.
Was the inspector a local man, or was he sent by the department
I have not the name of the inspector.
His name is J. C. Wieder-hold.

When we were discussing public buildings before I stated that in some cases the clerk of works got $3 a day, in other cases $3.50, and in some cases $4. That man, as my deputy tells me, is not paid for Sundays ; therefore he gets a little extra pay per day.
I want to draw the minister's attention to the town of Oampbellford on the Trent canal.
If we were to erect all the buildings we have in the estimates and all that are asked for by hon. gentlemen opposite we would exceed the revenue.
The postal revenue of Camp-bellford is $3,500, money orders issued $15,000, and money orders paid $11,000.
What is the population?

Three thousand. I have not a statement of the customs revenue, but it is in the neighbourhood of $12,000. The Trent Valley canal will be completed through that part of the country within three or four years and we expect then to bloom into a city. It would be a very deplorable thing if Oampbellford should bloom into a city with such a progressive government as we have and we found we had no public building.
The hon. gentleman expects it will bloom into a city. How does the operation take place?
When the Trent Valley canal is completed we expect to bloom into a city. We are developing in the neighbourhood of 25,000 and 30,000 horse-power.

Have you any flour mills there?
Mr. PUGSLEY

Yes, and a large woollen mill, but, I regret to say, the woollen mill is running rather slack at present. We have a shoe factory, a sawmill, a planing mill and a sash factory. It is a very progressive town and a large amount of manufacturing is done there. At the present time we have to climb up a long stairs to the custom office and while the post office is moved to a more commodious building the accommodation is inadequate.
Is the custom house a public building?
No, we have no public building.

I am very glad to hear as to Oampbellford and if I have the opportunity of visiting that section of the country I will be very glad to look into the requirements of the place. It is not at all impossible that next session the wants of Oampbellford may receive favourable consideration.
If the minister comes to Oampbellford I will guarantee that we will give him a splendid time.
I am sure of that.

I was going to point out to my hon. friend from East Northumberland (Mr. Owen) that he might save his breath in regard to asking the minister what he shall do next session, looking forward to the time when the blooming process shall take place in Oampbellford, be-caused by the time that Cambellford blooms forth as a city this present administration *will be out of power, his friends will have the locating of post offices throughout the country and this town of Oampbellford will be looked after.
The minister said that if we only had patience for a short time all these things would come right; I suppose he had in view the change which is likely to take place in the administration.
We have three customs ports in East Elgin and the revenue amounts to $108,000. Aylmer is the centre of East Elgin and it is a very important place.
There are a great many important towns in Ontario.

I cannot help thinking that the minister would expedite matters if he would just be honest with the opposition and tell us that he did not intend to give one hon. member on this side of the House a public building in his riding. I am satisfied that the minister has not taken into consideration the granting of any public buildings to the constituencies represented by members of the opposition.
I do not agree with that.
He may have taken it into consideration, but he does not propose to do anything.

My kon. friend is doing me a wrong in that respect. Two or three days ago, when the hon. member for Kings and Albert rose and spoke of a public building at Hillsborough, I. while expressing my regret that the hon. gentleman had not approached me on the subject, told him that others had urged it very strongly and that X had the matter under favourable consideration. I may say to my hon. friend that there are quite a number of counties which are represented by our friends opposite in regard to which I recognize the claims which the people have for consideration in the way of public buildings, and I intend, If I remain Minister of Public Works, to take these claims into favourable consideration.

I am very glad to hear the minister make the remark he has. I think from the manner in which he says it that he means what he says. If he takes it into consideration a town such as Camp-bellford and the one represented by my hon. friend from Haldimand with several thousand of a population and large revenues. I am sure that he cannot consistently refuse to consider their claims, although, when I remember that in some of the Quebec constituencies, towns and villages of 500 and 600 people are receiving $20,000 buildings I cannot help thinking that there is not likely to be a very great deal of expenditure in some of the Ontario towns.
I see that $262.78 was expended for advertising for tenders for this building at St. Mary's. Would the minister bring down the list of the papers and the amount paid to each?

Certainly.
Sarnia public building-alterations and additions, $5,000.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. This is to make provision for the completion of the construction of a brick addition 53 by 25 feet to the Sarnia public building alterations. The total estimated cost is $14,999.22.
What amount of money was expended previously?
The amount to the 24th of December, was $5,426.22.

What has been the total cost of the building?
Mr. PUGSLEY'. I have not that. I suppose the original building was constructed quite a number of years ago.
No. just two years ago.
Is this the Sarnia post office?
Yes.
It is purely a post office.
No, because the addition involves alterations to the roof of the examining warehouse.
When originally constructed it was not intended for any other purpose than that of a post office.
It is used as an examining warehouse. The cost to the 30th June, 1906, was $73,915.78.
I remember being m that building once and I thought it was a miserable small place, altogether insufficient for the requirements of Sarnia.
It is used for post office, custom house, inland revenue, examining warehouse and the Indian agent. It is 99 feet on one street and 73 feet on another.

Then it must be altogether a different building from that I have in mind. I remember when Sir Wm. Mulock was Postmaster General discussing the matter and my remarks were endorsed by Dr. Johnston who then represented the constituency.
What will this extension to the building be used for.

It will be used in connection with some of the various services accommodated there.
Simooe public buildings, $10,000.

This is in the county of Norfolk. Now, here is a constituency represented by one of the hon. gentlemen opposite, which illustrates the fact that we are endeavouring to meet the wants of the public irrespective of the views of the representative.
Carried.
Let those Toronto items stand, until the members for the city are present.
I am quite willing to do so if the hon. gentleman desires. I move that the vote for the Toronto custom house be dropped.
Why?

It is all paid for in the past year; the work is completed.
>
Welland public building, $20,000.
The lot here is known as the market site and has a frontage of 58 feet on one street and 150 feet on another street.
What did you pay for the lot?

It was owned by the corporation of the town of Welland and the

price was $6,000. The town reserves at the rear of the town hall a strip of land for a driveway to be held In common with the town.
What was the total cost of the building?
The plans have not yet been completed, but it is supposed it will cost about $30,000.
Why don't you keep it within $20,000?

This is the estimate of the chief architect. I will try to keep it down to $20,000 exclusive of the site, but it will be pretty difficult to do that. This is to be for customs as well.
Mr. FOW'LER. Why don't you keep it down to $20,000?

1 don't like to set up my judgment against that of the chief architect. Welland has a population of about 4,500 and within last year it has increased by between 1,500 and 2,000. It is moving ahead very rapidly. Last year the Plymouth Cordage Company which will employ 400 hands spent $300,000 there.
Do you allow the chief architect to say what shall be the cost of a public building?
No; but I respect his judgment.

The chief architect may have judgment with respect to drawing plans, but with respect to the requirements of the different towns throughout the country I would not consider the chief architect's opinion was worth a cent. It is the minister who is responsible for that.
The chief architect gets information as to what accommodation is required for the present and for the future.

No doubt we will be told that the chief architect will take the $8,000 salary and the minister will take the chief arcnitect's salary. I was astounded to hear the minister say that he had to give attention to the chief architect as to what amount of money should be spent by the government in any particular place. Surely the minister spoke these words without consideration.
No, that was said deliberately.
Then I regret it* very much. The minister should be responsible for the expenditure.
So he is.

Not if he allows his chief architect to overrule him. The minister should be in a position to say to the chief architect: I want you to draw plans for a building costing so many thousand Mr. PUGSLEY.
dollars, and all the architect should have to say about it is to draw the plans. If he did that, the chief architect would have obeyed his order, and the minister would be surprised, when the building was erected, what a beautiful building he would get for that amount of money. The country wTill be surprised when they read that the minister has acceded to the officers of his department the right to say how much the expenditure of this country is to be.
It is delightful to see the serious countenance of my hon. friend when he knows that he is only joking.
No, I am absolutely serious.'

I think it would be absurd for me to say to the chief architect, they want a post office in Montreal and I want you to spend $50,(100 ou it, or they want a post office at Ottawa and I want you to spend $25,000 on it. What we do is this. The chief architect finds out what the requirements of a town are, considers what its present population is and whether it is a growing town or not, and is then able to judge what accommodation is required, and he makes his estimate accordingly. When it comes to my hands, I cut it down as much as possible. At the same time I want him to erect a building which will be a credit to the government and not a discredit to the town. I am quite ready to admit that I. am advised by the chief architect and the chief engineer and the deputy, for whose judgments I have great respect.

The town of Welland I know very well ; the county of Welland adjoins my county, and I quite agree with the minister when he says that Welland is a growing and prosperous town. I do not know any town that is growing as fast. I think the expenditure of $20,000 in Welland is a necessary and very wise expenditure, very much more so than an expenditure of $40,000 in St. Mary's or $90,000 in Owen Sound.
Not at all. We have found that the chief architect has a staff of twelve architects besides himself,- and that in addition over $100,000 was spent last year for architects.
Oh. no.

I say, oh, yes. This is the man who decides whether a public building shall be built in a certain town or not and what money shall be spent on it, and the minister meekly bows his head and confirms whatever statement he makes.
That is not exactly what I said.

The hon. minister left us to infer that, and knowing what a mild man he is, I am sure he bows his head with grace and meekness. I venture to say that even in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, the subordinates have not quite so great control over the minister.

It strikes me that my hon. friend's remarks are not founded on reason. Surely if a wharf is to be constructed, it would be absurd for me to say to the chief engineer, I want you to see that a wharf is built that will cost $10,000. What I ask him to do is to examine the site, find out the depth of water, the size of the steamers which will use the wharf, what frontage is required and how far the wharf should extend into the water and then give an estimate of the cost. And if he should estimate that a wharf suitable to the requirements will cost $10,000, it would be absurd for me to limit the expenditure to $5,000. In the same way, when a public building is required, I have to get the chief architect to examine into the details and make his estimates according to the requirements. And if a public building requires a certain number of offices, it would be absurd for me to order one with insufficient accommodation. I have to be guided by the report of my chief architect.
